text:
save_trajectories()
Writes the simulated locations to outputs/deepSSF_trajectories/. The filename records how many trajectories, how many steps and the date, and the function never overwrites an existing file — re-running the cell appends a _2, _3, … run counter instead, so repeated runs accumulate rather than clobber.

Inputs:

trajectories — a DataFrame (or list of DataFrames)
output_dir — created if it doesn’t exist
prefix — leading part of the filename
split — write one file per trajectory_id instead of one combined file

Outputs: the list of paths written



Code
from deepssf import save_trajectories

TRAJ_DIR = OUTPUT_DIR / "deepSSF_trajectories"

save_trajectories(sim_df, TRAJ_DIR, prefix="deepSSF_pigs")

title: deepSSF Package Walkthrough
text:
simulate_trajectories()
Runs n_trajectories simulations and returns them stacked in one long-format DataFrame with trajectory_id and step columns.
Three methods are available:








method
how it works
when to use it




"batched" (default)
every trajectory takes its step together, so the model sees a batch of n_trajectories windows per forward pass instead of one
almost always — the forward pass is the whole cost of the simulation, and it is far better used at batch size 50 than at batch size 1


"sequential"
a plain loop over simulate_trajectory()
reference behaviour; needed if trajectories start at different times


"parallel"
the same loop across a thread pool
when start times vary and you want some overlap; the speed-up is modest (PyTorch releases the GIL inside its ops, but torch is already using several threads per op) and results are not reproducible from a seed



The one restriction on "batched" is that all trajectories share a clock, so starting_yday / starting_hour must be scalars. Start locations can still differ per trajectory — pass a list to start_x / start_y to release simulated animals from different points.


Code
from deepssf import simulate_trajectories

N_TRAJECTORIES = 10
N_SIM_STEPS = 1000

sim_many = simulate_trajectories(
    model,
    get_landscape=get_landscape,
    transform=raster_transform,
    start_x=start_x,
    start_y=start_y,
    n_steps=N_SIM_STEPS,
    n_trajectories=N_TRAJECTORIES,
    method="batched",
    starting_yday=test_sample["yday_t1"].iloc[0],
    starting_hour=test_sample["hour_t1"].iloc[0],
    time_between_steps=1.0,
    window_size=WINDOW_SIZE,
    month_index_fn=lambda _yday: 0,   # static layers
)
print(f"{sim_many['trajectory_id'].nunique()} trajectories x "
      f"{N_SIM_STEPS} steps = {len(sim_many):,} locations")
sim_many.head()



Releasing simulated animals from different starting points
Passing a sequence to start_x / start_y gives each simulated animal its own release site. Here we draw 10 observed locations at random and start one trajectory from each — the same batched forward pass, so it costs nothing extra.


Code
# Draw starting locations from the observed fixes
release = step_df.sample(N_TRAJECTORIES, random_state=42)

sim_scattered = simulate_trajectories(
    model,
    get_landscape=get_landscape,
    transform=raster_transform,
    start_x=release["x1_"].to_numpy(),
    start_y=release["y1_"].to_numpy(),
    n_steps=1000,
    n_trajectories=N_TRAJECTORIES,
    method="batched",
    starting_yday=test_sample["yday_t1"].iloc[0],
    starting_hour=test_sample["hour_t1"].iloc[0],
    window_size=WINDOW_SIZE,
    month_index_fn=lambda _yday: 0,
)
print(f"{len(sim_scattered):,} locations from {N_TRAJECTORIES} release sites")




Plot all of the simulated trajectories


Code
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 6))
for ax, df, title in zip(
    axes,
    [sim_many, sim_scattered],
    ["Same release site", "Random release sites"],
    strict=True,
):
    rasterio.plot.show(
        landscape_tensors[0].numpy(), transform=raster_transform, ax=ax, cmap="viridis"
    )
    ax.plot(
        step_df["x1_"], step_df["y1_"],
        "w.", alpha=0.2, markersize=0.5, label="observed",
    )
    # One colour per simulated individual
    for tid, sub in df.groupby("trajectory_id"):
        ax.plot(sub["x"], sub["y"], "-", linewidth=0.7, alpha=0.9, label=f"sim {tid}")
    ax.set_xlabel("Easting (m, projected)")
    ax.set_ylabel("Northing (m, projected)")
    ax.set_title(title)

plt.suptitle(f"{N_TRAJECTORIES} simulated trajectories")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig(str(OUTPUT_DIR / "simulated_trajectories.png"), dpi=100)
plt.show()

title: deepSSF Package Walkthrough
section: Create a heatmap of the simulated trajectories
text:
Create a heatmap of the simulated trajectories
Count the number of simulated locations per cell/pixel, with an option to discard the first n steps to reduce bias towards the initial parameters.

title: deepSSF Package Walkthrough
text:
trajectory_heatmap()

Inputs

trajectories

simulated locations, as returned by simulate_trajectories() (or a list of DataFrames).

transform, shape

the landscape rasters’ affine transform and (height, width), so the heatmap grid shares their origin and CRS.

burn_in

discard the first n steps of every trajectory. Early steps cluster around the release site(s) and reflect the starting conditions rather than the fitted model.

agg

aggregate agg x agg raster pixels into one heatmap cell. At the native 20 m almost every occupied cell holds a single location, so some coarsening makes the surface readable.


Outputs: (counts, heatmap_transform) — an int32 array of locations per cell, and its affine transform.

The result is visualised as a PNG below, written to a GeoTIFF with save_raster() so it can be opened in QGIS, and added to the interactive map as a layer that can be toggled on and off with add_heatmap_overlay().


Code
from deepssf import trajectory_heatmap

HEATMAP_DF   = sim_many  # trajectories to summarise (or sim_many)
BURN_IN      = 100            # drop the first n steps of every trajectory
HEATMAP_AGG  = 4              # heatmap cell = HEATMAP_AGG x HEATMAP_AGG raster pixels

heatmap, heatmap_transform = trajectory_heatmap(
    HEATMAP_DF,
    raster_transform,
    landscape_tensors[0].shape,
    burn_in=BURN_IN,
    agg=HEATMAP_AGG,
)

print(f"Heatmap grid: {heatmap.shape[0]} x {heatmap.shape[1]} cells of "
      f"{PIXEL_SIZE * HEATMAP_AGG:.0f} m")
print(f"{heatmap.sum():,} locations counted after dropping the first {BURN_IN} steps "
      f"of each trajectory")
print(f"{(heatmap > 0).sum():,} occupied cells, up to {heatmap.max():,} locations in one cell")



Plot the heatmap
Counts are drawn on a log colour scale — a handful of cells near the release sites usually hold an order of magnitude more locations than the rest, which would flatten a linear scale to a single bright dot. Empty cells are masked so the landscape shows through.


Code
from matplotlib.colors import LogNorm

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.5, 7))
# Greyscale background so the (colourful) heatmap stays readable on top
rasterio.plot.show(
    landscape_tensors[0].numpy(), transform=raster_transform, ax=ax, cmap="Greys_r"
)
ax.plot(
    step_df["x1_"], step_df["y1_"],
    "c.", alpha=0.15, markersize=0.5, label="observed",
)
img = ax.imshow(
    np.ma.masked_equal(heatmap, 0),  # empty cells stay transparent
    extent=rasterio.plot.plotting_extent(heatmap, heatmap_transform),
    cmap="magma",
    norm=LogNorm(vmin=1, vmax=max(int(heatmap.max()), 2)),
    interpolation="nearest",
    alpha=0.85,
)
fig.colorbar(img, ax=ax, label=f"simulated locations per {PIXEL_SIZE * HEATMAP_AGG:.0f} m cell")
ax.set_xlabel("Easting (m, projected)")
ax.set_ylabel("Northing (m, projected)")
ax.set_title(
    f"Simulated space use — {HEATMAP_DF['trajectory_id'].nunique()} trajectories, "
    f"steps {BURN_IN}+"
)
ax.legend(markerscale=8, loc="upper right")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig(str(OUTPUT_DIR / "simulated_heatmap.png"), dpi=150)
plt.show()




Save the heatmap as a raster (TIF)

title: deepSSF Package Walkthrough
text:
save_raster()
Writes any landscape-shaped array out as a GeoTIFF, given the transform and CRS that georeference it — the heatmap here, or the habitat selection surface above. nodata=0 means unvisited cells are drawn as transparent rather than as a solid zero-valued block.


Code
from deepssf import save_raster

# load_environmental_layers() does not return the CRS, so read it off the source
# raster the transform came from.
with rasterio.open(next(iter(LAYER_PATHS.values()))) as src:
    raster_crs = src.crs

heatmap_tif = save_raster(
    heatmap,
    OUTPUT_DIR
    / f"simulated_heatmap_{HEATMAP_DF['trajectory_id'].nunique()}traj"
      f"_{PIXEL_SIZE * HEATMAP_AGG:.0f}m_burnin{BURN_IN}.tif",
    transform=heatmap_transform,
    crs=raster_crs,
    nodata=0,               # cells never visited
    band_descriptions="simulated locations per cell",
)



Toggle the heatmap on the interactive map

title: deepSSF Package Walkthrough
text:
add_heatmap_overlay()
plot_trajectories_folium() returns the folium.Map, so the heatmap can be added to it afterwards as an image overlay. folium builds the layer control when the map renders, so the heatmap picks up its own checkbox alongside the observed locations and each simulated trajectory.
The counts are warped from the projected CRS to Web Mercator — the projection Leaflet stretches an overlay in — and coloured with the same log scale as the PNG, with cells below vmin (1 by default) left fully transparent.


Code
from deepssf import add_heatmap_overlay

fmap_heat = plot_trajectories_folium(
    HEATMAP_DF,
    observed=step_df,
    src_crs="EPSG:3112",
    basemap="esri_imagery",
    zoom_start=11,
    max_observed_points=100000,
)
add_heatmap_overlay(
    fmap_heat,
    heatmap,
    heatmap_transform,
    src_crs="EPSG:3112",
    name=f"heatmap (max {heatmap.max():,} per cell)",
    cmap="magma",
    opacity=0.75,
)

heatmap_html = OUTPUT_DIR / "simulated_heatmap_map.html"
fmap_heat.save(str(heatmap_html))
print(f"Map saved: {heatmap_html}")
fmap_heat



The same trajectories on the interactive map
Each trajectory gets its own colour and its own entry in the layer control (top right), so individual animals can be switched on and off.


Code
plot_trajectories_folium(
    sim_many,
    observed=step_df,
    src_crs="EPSG:3112",
    basemap="esri_imagery",
    zoom_start=11,
    max_observed_points = 100000,
    save_path=str(OUTPUT_DIR / "simulated_trajectories_map.html"),
)




Save them all
split=False (the default) writes one combined CSV with the trajectory_id column; split=True writes one file per simulated individual.


Code
save_trajectories(sim_many, TRAJ_DIR, prefix="deepSSF_pigs")

# ...or one file per simulated animal:
# save_trajectories(sim_many, TRAJ_DIR, prefix="deepSSF_pigs", split=True)




How much faster is "batched"?
Batching wins by more as n_trajectories grows, because a forward pass at batch size 1 leaves most of the GPU (or most of the CPU’s vector units) idle — running 50 trajectories together costs barely more per step than running one. On an Apple M-series GPU (mps), 200 steps with WINDOW_SIZE = 75:










n_trajectories
"batched"
"sequential"
"parallel"
speed-up




4
1.5 s
3.3 s
3.0 s
2.2x


16
2.0 s
14.1 s
12.1 s
6.9x


64
1.6 s
54.4 s
48.9 s
34x



Note that "parallel" is only ~10% quicker than "sequential" here: torch is already spreading each convolution across cores, so extra Python threads have little left to win. Worth re-running on your own hardware.


Code
import time

BENCH_TRAJ, BENCH_STEPS = 100, 100

for method in ("batched", "sequential", "parallel"):
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    _ = simulate_trajectories(
        model,
        get_landscape=get_landscape,
        transform=raster_transform,
        start_x=start_x,
        start_y=start_y,
        n_steps=BENCH_STEPS,
        n_trajectories=BENCH_TRAJ,
        method=method,
        starting_yday=test_sample["yday_t1"].iloc[0],
        starting_hour=test_sample["hour_t1"].iloc[0],
        window_size=WINDOW_SIZE,
        month_index_fn=lambda _yday: 0,
    )
    elapsed = time.perf_counter() - t0
    print(f"{method:11s} {elapsed:6.2f} s "
          f"({BENCH_TRAJ * BENCH_STEPS / elapsed:7.0f} steps/s)")

title: Data Preparation
text:
Creating a step object


Show code
# nest the data by individual
pig_all_nested <- pig_all %>% arrange(id) %>% nest(data = -"id")

pig_all_nested_steps <- pig_all_nested %>%
  mutate(steps = map(data, function(x)
    x %>% track_resample(rate = minutes(30), tolerance = minutes(65)) %>%
      steps_by_burst(keep_cols = "start")))

# unnest the data after creating 'steps' objects
pig_all_steps <- pig_all_nested_steps %>% 
  amt::select(id, steps) %>% 
  amt::unnest(cols = steps) %>% 
  relocate(c(name, n_sat), .before = id) %>% 
  mutate(dt_min = as.numeric(difftime(t2_, t1_, units = "mins")),
         dt_hour = as.numeric(difftime(t2_, t1_, units = "hours"))) %>% 
  filter(dt_min > 20)

hist(as.numeric(pig_all_steps$dt_min))

# simplified names for the BOM weather variables (new name = original BOM name), used for both stations
weather_names <- c(
  rain_since_9am_mm = "Precipitation since 9am local time in mm",
  air_temp_c = "Air Temperature in degrees C",
  wet_bulb_temp_c = "Wet bulb temperature in degrees C",
  dew_point_temp_c = "Dew point temperature in degrees C",
  rel_humidity_pct = "Relative humidity in percentage %",
  wind_speed_kmh = "Wind speed in km/h",
  wind_dir_deg = "Wind direction in degrees true",
  max_gust_10min_kmh = "Speed of maximum windgust in last 10 minutes in  km/h",
  cloud_amount_1 = "Ceilometer cloud amount (of first group)",
  cloud_height_1_ft = "Ceilometer cloud height (of first group) in feet",
  cloud_amount_2 = "Ceilometer cloud amount (of second group)",
  cloud_height_2_ft = "Ceilometer cloud height (of second group) in feet",
  cloud_amount_3 = "Ceilometer cloud amount (of third group)",
  cloud_height_3_ft = "Ceilometer cloud height (of third group) in feet",
  sky_clear_flag = "Ceilometer sky clear flag"
)

# the original names are used as plot labels, plus a label for the derived half-hourly rain
weather_labels <- c(weather_names,
                    rain_30min_mm = "Precipitation in the previous 30 minutes in mm")
weather_labels[] <- stringr::str_squish(weather_labels) # removes the double space in the gust name

# save the labels for the analysis scripts
write_csv(tibble::enframe(weather_labels, name = "variable", value = "label"),
          "data/weather_variable_labels.csv")

oenpelli_weather <- oenpelli_weather_full %>%
  dplyr::select(-hm, -`Station Number`, -matches("quality", ignore.case = TRUE),
                -matches("Ceilometer"), -`AWS Flag`, -`#`) %>%
  # combine the date/time components, which are in local standard time (Darwin has no daylight saving)
  dplyr::mutate(
    datetime = lubridate::make_datetime(
      year = `Year Month Day Hour Minutes in YYYY`,
      month = as.integer(MM),
      day = as.integer(DD),
      hour = as.integer(HH24),
      min = as.integer(`MI format in Local standard time`),
      tz = "Australia/Darwin"),
    .before = 1) %>%
  dplyr::select(-`Year Month Day Hour Minutes in YYYY`, -MM, -DD, -HH24,
                -`MI format in Local standard time`) %>%
  # any_of() as the cloud columns aren't recorded at Oenpelli
  dplyr::rename(dplyr::any_of(weather_names)) %>%
  # rain in each half-hour - the since-9am total resets after the 9:00 reading, so group by
  # rain day (9:30 to 9:00 the next day) and subtract the previous reading
  dplyr::mutate(rain_day = lubridate::as_date(datetime - lubridate::minutes(570))) %>%
  dplyr::group_by(rain_day) %>%
  # round to remove floating point error from the subtraction (gauge resolution is 0.2 mm)
  dplyr::mutate(rain_30min_mm = round(rain_since_9am_mm - dplyr::lag(rain_since_9am_mm, default = 0), 1),
                .after = rain_since_9am_mm) %>%
  dplyr::ungroup() %>%
  dplyr::select(-rain_day) %>%
  dplyr::rename_with(~ paste0("onpli_", .x))

title: Earth Engine imagery for the feral pig tracking AOI
text:
The workflow is:

Read the step data (data/pig_all_steps_*.csv), which is in EPSG:3112 (GDA94 / Geoscience Australia Lambert).
Take the bounding box of all step start and end coordinates, buffer it by 10 km, and turn it into an ee.Geometry (the AOI).
Take the temporal range of the tracking data (t1_ to t2_) and build a median cloud-free Sentinel-2 composite over that window, using the Cloud Score+ mask.
Derive NDVI and NDWI from the same composite.
Grab the AlphaEarth / Satellite Embedding annual image (64 bands) for a chosen year.
Export each product, either locally to mapping/ (small rasters) or to the Google Drive folder feral_pig_mapping (anything bigger).

Everything you are likely to want to change lives in the Configuration cell.

title: Earth Engine imagery for the feral pig tracking AOI
text:
Temporal extent
The Sentinel-2 composite covers the full span of the tracking data. PAD_DAYS lets you widen that window (useful if the tracking period is short and the wet season leaves you with too few clear observations).


Show the code
# Parse every timestamp column and take the overall min/max.
times = pd.concat([pd.to_datetime(tracks[c], utc=True) for c in TIME_COLS])
track_start, track_end = times.min(), times.max()

start_date = (track_start - timedelta(days=PAD_DAYS)).strftime('%Y-%m-%d')
# +1 day because Earth Engine's filterDate() end is exclusive.
end_date = (track_end + timedelta(days=PAD_DAYS + 1)).strftime('%Y-%m-%d')

print(f"Tracking period:  {track_start:%Y-%m-%d} to {track_end:%Y-%m-%d}")
print(f"Imagery window:   {start_date} to {end_date} (end exclusive)")

title: Habitat Selection Explorer
text:
How strongly does the fitted deepSSF model select each part of the landscape at different times of day, seasons and weather? Pick an hour, a season and a weather preset to see the model’s habitat-selection surface, and the log selection ratio of each landcover class.

What is mapped: the habitat surface of the fitted model (the habitat head only, so every cell is treated as reachable), within 500 m of an observed fix. Brighter cells are more strongly selected. The colour scale is the same for every preset, so maps can be compared directly.
Weather presets: real half-hours observed at the Oenpelli station in that season (same month), within an hour of the chosen time:

cool & dry and hot & humid: the 10th and 90th percentiles of wet bulb temperature, without rain;
typical: closest to the median of every weather variable;
rain: the median rain amount among half-hours with rain. There is none in the early dry season, and only some hours in the late dry season have it.

Bar chart: the log selection ratio within the mask. 0 means the class is used in proportion to its availability; positive values mean it is selected for.

The maps are precomputed (347 scenarios). The methods, and partial dependence plots that separate the effects of time and weather, are in the deepSSF Inference notebook. A local app that recomputes maps for any time and weather is described in apps/README.md.




 Back to top

This notebook uses the fitted deepSSF model (landcover + weather covariates) to ask how the model’s predictions respond to its inputs:
The model-based results are meant to be compared with the empirical, binned versions in the weather analysis. The setup below is the same as in the prediction notebook.

title: deepSSF Inference
section: Set random seed and the device for predicting from the model
text:
Set random seed and the device for predicting from the model
If you have a GPU, this is where it will be specified (automatically).


Show code
# Reproducibility — fix random seeds so results are the same on every run.
# Prediction is not deterministic: simulate_trajectory() samples a next location
# from the predicted probability surface at every step, so without a seed two
# runs of the same trained model give different trajectories (and a different
# heatmap).  Seeding here makes a set of simulations reproducible.
torch.manual_seed(42)
np.random.seed(42)

# DEVICE is capitalised — module-level constant (set once, never reassigned).
# get_device() returns 'cuda' if a GPU is available, 'mps' on Apple Silicon,
# or 'cpu' otherwise.  All tensors and the model are moved to this device.
DEVICE = deepssf.get_device()
print(f"Device: {DEVICE}")


Device: mps

title: deepSSF Inference
text:
Set script paths
These must point at the same data and rasters the model was trained on — the model takes one input channel per raster band, in LAYER_PATHS order, so a different set of layers (or a different order) either fails to load the weights or feeds the wrong covariate into each filter.
OUTPUT_DIR is the directory a training run wrote its checkpoints to, given here as a literal path rather than through get_output_dir() (which mints a new dated directory). Figures and rasters produced below are written back into the same directory, alongside the model they came from.
All-caps names below are module-level constants — set once here and referenced throughout the notebook without being reassigned. Python has no built-in constant keyword, so capitalisation is the community convention (PEP 8) to signal “do not change this value”.


Show code
DATA_DIR = Path("data")  # location of the bundled sample data
MAPPING_DIR = Path("mapping")  # location of the landcover mapping files
CSV_PATH = DATA_DIR / "pigs_east_alligator_steps_covs_20261015.csv"  # GPS tracking data, 28 individuals

# Must match LAYER_PATHS in deepssf_piggies_train_landcover.ipynb, in the same order.
# NOTE: 's2' and 's2_dir' are RESERVED keys in load_environmental_layers().
# 's2_dir' triggers the monthly-composite loader (load_s2_data), and a plain
# 's2' entry is skipped by the per-file loop — so a single multi-band GeoTIFF
# must be given any *other* name, otherwise nothing is loaded and the function
# raises "raster_transform could not be set".
LAYER_PATHS = {
    # Topographic layers (DEM, slope)
    "dem": str(MAPPING_DIR / "DEM_east_alligator_3112.tif"),
    "slope": str(MAPPING_DIR / "slope_east_alligator_3112.tif"),

    # Categorical landcover layers (one-hot encoded)
    "landcover": str(MAPPING_DIR / "landcover_dummy_east_alligator.tif"),
}

# The training run to predict from — where its checkpoints and scaling
# coefficients were written by deepssf_piggies_train_landcover.ipynb.
OUTPUT_DIR = Path("outputs/landcover/2026-11-17_1")
CKPT_PATH = OUTPUT_DIR / "best_model.pt"
SCALING_PATH = OUTPUT_DIR / "scalar_scaling.csv"  # weather-covariate scaling used in training

for path in (CKPT_PATH, SCALING_PATH):
    if not path.exists():
        raise FileNotFoundError(
            f"No {path.name} in {OUTPUT_DIR} — set OUTPUT_DIR to a directory that "
            "deepssf_piggies_train_landcover.ipynb has finished writing to."
        )
# Inference results (CSVs and PNGs) go in one subdirectory per stage of this
# directory.  outputs/ is gitignored; figures are also kept in the notebook.
INFERENCE_DIR = OUTPUT_DIR / "inference"
INFERENCE_DIR.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

print(f"Output directory: {OUTPUT_DIR}")
print(f"Inference outputs: {INFERENCE_DIR}")
print("Checkpoints:", ", ".join(sorted(p.name for p in OUTPUT_DIR.glob("*.pt"))))


Output directory: outputs/landcover/2026-11-17_1
Inference outputs: outputs/landcover/2026-11-17_1/inference
Checkpoints: best_model.pt, best_model_habitat.pt, best_model_movement.pt

title: deepSSF Inference
text:
load_environmental_layers()
Reads each GeoTIFF listed in LAYER_PATHS, min–max

Scales every band to [0, 1], and returns:

env_layers — dict mapping layer name → NumPy array: 2-D (H × W) for single-band GeoTIFFs, 3-D (bands × H × W) for multi-band ones, where each band becomes its own model input channel
raster_transform — Affine object that converts pixel (row, col) indices to the projected coordinates (easting, northing) of the raster(s), which should be in the same CRS as the GPS data. This transform is used whenever we need to translate between pixel space and real-world coordinates.


Two things to watch for:

The keys 's2' and 's2_dir' are reserved for the monthly Sentinel-2 composite loader — a single GeoTIFF passed under the name 's2' is silently skipped (see the note in the paths cell above).
The rescaling uses a single global min/max across all bands of a file, and computes (data - lo) / hi rather than (data - lo) / (hi - lo). Our index raster is int16 scaled by 10 000 with ±10 000 fill values, so the loaded values span [0, 2] rather than [0, 1] and the three indices are not individually normalised. That is workable (the CNN can rescale internally) but if it hurts training, pre-scale each band yourself and save as .npy — non-.tif paths in LAYER_PATHS are loaded with np.load(..., mmap_mode='r') and left untouched, though at least one real .tif must remain in the dict so the transform can be set.

title: deepSSF Inference
text:
SCALAR_COLS
These are non-spatial inputs. For processing with convolutional layers, they are converted into spatial windows (rasters/arrays), and stacked with the truly spatial covariates.
The model receives a fixed-size spatial window centred on each step’s start location. To let the network express time-varying habitat preferences (e.g. different nocturnal vs diurnal use), scalar covariates are tiled into additional channels of the same H × W size, so every pixel “knows” the current time context when habitat suitability is estimated.

hour_t1_sin1 / hour_t1_cos1

Sine and cosine of (2π × hour / 24), encoding time-of-day as a circular variable. The circular encoding means 23:00 and 01:00 are treated as adjacent — a plain hour value would have an artificial discontinuity at midnight.

yday_t1_sin1 / yday_t1_cos1

Same circular encoding for day-of-year (1–365), capturing seasonal variation in habitat use (e.g. dry-season vs wet-season movements).

dt_hour

Elapsed time between consecutive fixes (hours). Because GPS collars do not always fix at a perfectly regular rate, including dt_hour lets the movement kernel rescale expected displacement proportionally to the actual time interval rather than assuming a fixed fix rate. Note: dt_hour must be supplied at simulation time as well, so that simulate_trajectory() produces inputs consistent with training.

Weather covariates from the onpli_ weather station, carried over from the CSV for the start of each step:

rain_30min_mm, air_temp_c, wet_bulb_temp_c, dew_point_temp_c, rel_humidity_pct, wind_speed_kmh

Standardised to z-scores (the *_scaled columns) before going into the model, with rain log-transformed, log(1 + x), first. The mean and SD are kept so model inputs and effects can be converted back to natural units.

wind_dir_deg

Encoded as a sine/cosine pair (onpli_wind_dir_sin1 / onpli_wind_dir_cos1) for the same wraparound reason as hour of day, with calm steps set to (0, 0).



These must match SCALAR_COLS in the training notebook — same columns, same order.


Show code
# Time covariates derived by prepare_movement_df().  Not scaled: the sin/cos pairs
# are already in [-1, 1], and simulate_trajectory() fills dt_hour with the raw
# time_between_steps (hours), so the model has to be trained on raw hours too.
TIME_COLS = ["hour_t1_sin1",
             "hour_t1_cos1",
             "yday_t1_sin1",
             "yday_t1_cos1",
             "dt_hour"]

# Weather covariates carried over from the CSV in natural units, and standardised
# to z-scores further down (the "_scaled" columns)
WEATHER_COLS = ["onpli_rain_30min_mm",
                "onpli_air_temp_c",
                "onpli_wet_bulb_temp_c",
                "onpli_dew_point_temp_c",
                "onpli_rel_humidity_pct",
                "onpli_wind_speed_kmh"
                ]

# Wind direction (degrees) is carried over, then encoded as a sin/cos pair further
# down rather than scaled
WIND_DIR_COL = "onpli_wind_dir_deg"

# The model inputs, in the order the model sees them
SCALAR_COLS = (
    TIME_COLS
    + [f"{col}_scaled" for col in WEATHER_COLS]
    + ["onpli_wind_dir_sin1", "onpli_wind_dir_cos1"]
)
print(f"{len(SCALAR_COLS)} scalar inputs: {SCALAR_COLS}")

title: deepSSF Inference
text:
prepare_movement_df()
Converts a fixes dataframe (one row per GPS location) into a step dataframe (one row per movement between consecutive fixes).

For each step it computes:

dx, dy — displacement in projected CRS units (metres)
bearing — direction of travel (radians; 0 = north, clockwise positive)
bearing_tm1 — bearing of the previous step, used as a model input so the network can capture directional persistence by estimating a turning angle
dt_hour — time elapsed between consecutive fixes (hours)
hour_t1, yday_t1 — decimal hour-of-day and day-of-year at the step start location
*_sin1 / *_cos1 — sine/cosine encodings of hour and yday (see SCALAR_COLS below)


The “1” on column names (x1_, y1_, t1_, etc.) flags them as “start of step” variables; and the “2” in x2_, y2_, t2_ are the corresponding “end of step” values, following the convention of the amt package (Signer et al. 2019). The last fix for each individual is dropped because no forward step can be formed.


Show code

# let it re-form the steps from consecutive fixes.

    raw_df, 
    id_col="name", 
    time_col="t1_", 
    x_col="x1_", 
    y_col="y1_",

    scalar_cols=TIME_COLS + WEATHER_COLS + [WIND_DIR_COL],
)

Encode wind direction as a sin/cos pair
Wind direction follows the BoM convention: the compass bearing the wind blows from, in 10° steps clockwise from north (90 = from the east). North is recorded as 360, and 0 is reserved for calm (no wind, so no direction).
Taking the sine and cosine removes the wraparound, so 350° and 10° sit next to each other and 0° and 360° both mean north: - onpli_wind_dir_sin1 — east–west component (+1 = from the east, −1 = from the west) - onpli_wind_dir_cos1 — north–south component (+1 = from the north, −1 = from the south)
Calm steps are set to (0, 0). A plain sin/cos of 0° gives (0, 1), which the model would read as a northerly. wind_dir_from_sin_cos() converts back to 0–360° (0 = north), returning NaN for calm.


Show code
def wind_dir_to_sin_cos(deg):
    """Compass degrees (0 = north, clockwise) -> (sin, cos)."""
    rad = np.radians(np.asarray(deg, dtype=float))
    return np.sin(rad), np.cos(rad)


def wind_dir_from_sin_cos(sin1, cos1):
    """(sin, cos) -> compass degrees in [0, 360), 0 = north.  NaN for calm (0, 0)."""
    sin1 = np.asarray(sin1, dtype=float)
    cos1 = np.asarray(cos1, dtype=float)
    # Round before wrapping so north comes back as 0 rather than 359.99999...
    deg = np.round(np.degrees(np.arctan2(sin1, cos1)), 6) % 360
    return np.where(np.hypot(sin1, cos1) < 1e-6, np.nan, deg)


calm = (step_df[WIND_DIR_COL] == 0).to_numpy()   # BoM code for calm
wind_sin, wind_cos = wind_dir_to_sin_cos(step_df[WIND_DIR_COL])
step_df["onpli_wind_dir_sin1"] = np.where(calm, 0.0, wind_sin)
step_df["onpli_wind_dir_cos1"] = np.where(calm, 0.0, wind_cos)

Scale the weather covariates with the training coefficients
The model was trained on weather covariates scaled with a particular transform, mean and SD (rain log-transformed, log(1 + x), then every covariate converted to a z-score). Any input to the model has to be scaled the same way, so the coefficients are loaded from scalar_scaling.csv, which the training notebook saved in OUTPUT_DIR, rather than recalculated here.

scale_covariate(values, col) converts natural units to the model’s scale, e.g. for weather values set by hand for a prediction.
unscale_covariate(values, col) converts back to natural units: natural = scaled × SD + mean, followed by exp(x) − 1 for log1p columns.

As a check, the coefficients are also recalculated from the data loaded here. They should match, unless the data or the NA handling has changed since the model was trained.


Show code
# Transform, mean and SD for each weather covariate, as used in training
SCALING = pd.read_csv(SCALING_PATH, index_col="column")
missing = [col for col in WEATHER_COLS if col not in SCALING.index]
if missing:
    raise KeyError(f"{SCALING_PATH} has no scaling for {missing}")
print("Scaling coefficients (from training):")
print(SCALING.round(3).to_string())


def scale_covariate(values, col):
    """Natural units -> model scale for `col`: log1p if listed, then z-score."""
    values = np.asarray(values, dtype=float)
    if SCALING.at[col, "transform"] == "log1p":
        values = np.log1p(values)
    return (values - SCALING.at[col, "mean"]) / SCALING.at[col, "sd"]


def unscale_covariate(values, col):
    """Model scale -> natural units for `col`: undo the z-score, then expm1 if logged."""
    values = np.asarray(values, dtype=float) * SCALING.at[col, "sd"] + SCALING.at[col, "mean"]
    if SCALING.at[col, "transform"] == "log1p":
        values = np.expm1(values)
    return values


for col in WEATHER_COLS:
    step_df[f"{col}_scaled"] = scale_covariate(step_df[col], col)

# Check: recalculating the coefficients from this notebook's data gives the same
# values as the training run
for col in WEATHER_COLS:
    values = step_df[col].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    if SCALING.at[col, "transform"] == "log1p":
        values = np.log1p(values)
    if not np.allclose([values.mean(), values.std(ddof=1)],
                       SCALING.loc[col, ["mean", "sd"]].to_numpy(dtype=float)):
        print(f"Warning: {col} mean/SD differ from training — has the data or NA "
              "handling changed since the model was trained?")
        break
else:
    print("\nCoefficients recalculated from this data match the training run.")

filter_steps_by_window()
Removes steps whose straight-line displacement exceeds half the spatial window (WINDOW_SIZE × PIXEL_SIZE / 2 metres). Such steps would place the true next location outside the predicted probability map, causing an index error in the loss function.


Show code

    step_df, window_size=WINDOW_SIZE, pixel_size=PIXEL_SIZE
)

title: deepSSF Inference
text:
params_from_checkpoint()
Weights only load into a model built with the same architecture, so predicting from a trained model means reproducing its hyper-parameters exactly. Rather than re-typing the training notebook’s constants here — where a habitat branch one layer too shallow fails loudly, but a mis-set pixel_size quietly rescales the movement kernel — params_from_checkpoint() recovers them from the checkpoint and returns the ModelParams to hand to ConvJointModel.
deepssf writes the ModelParams dict into every checkpoint, so for a model trained with 0.3.1 or later it is simply read back. Older checkpoints (anything in outputs/ trained before then) do not have it, and the architecture is recovered from the layer shapes instead: a conv weight is [out_channels, in_channels, k, k] and a linear weight [out_features, in_features], which between them pin down every hyper-parameter that changes a tensor shape — input_channels, output_channels, kernel_size, both conv-layer counts, dense_dim_in_all, dense_dim_hidden and num_movement_params. Either way the result is checked against the saved tensors, so a stored params dict that contradicts its own weights raises here rather than failing later inside load_state_dict.
Three things it cannot get from the file, passed in below:

image_dim — the habitat branch is fully convolutional, so nothing in the weights records the training window. The movement branch’s flattened size does constrain it, and that is checked, but only to within the slack that max-pooling’s floor division allows (48–55 px all flatten to the same 288 here). WINDOW_SIZE also has to match filter_steps_by_window() above, and is the window the simulations step within.
pixel_size — a property of the raster, read off raster_transform.
device — where the model is being run, which has nothing to do with where it was trained; it defaults to this machine rather than to the recorded value.

n_scalar_covariates only fills the two ModelParams fields that no layer reads; the scalar count that matters is folded into input_channels, which comes off the weights. The check below is the one thing the checkpoint cannot do for us — that the covariates loaded in this notebook are the ones the model was trained on. It compares counts only, so keep LAYER_PATHS in the training run’s order.


Show code
params = deepssf.params_from_checkpoint(
    str(CKPT_PATH),
    image_dim=WINDOW_SIZE,               # not recorded in the weights
    pixel_size=PIXEL_SIZE,               # from raster_transform
    n_scalar_covariates=len(SCALAR_COLS),
    device=DEVICE,                       # this machine, not the training machine
)
for name, value in params.to_dict().items():
    print(f"  {name:26s}: {value}")

# The covariates in this notebook must be the ones the model was trained on.
# input_channels is one channel per raster band plus one per scalar covariate,
# so a changed LAYER_PATHS or SCALAR_COLS shows up here as a count mismatch.
n_expected = N_SPATIAL_CHANNELS + len(SCALAR_COLS)
if n_expected != params.input_channels:
    raise ValueError(
        f"{N_SPATIAL_CHANNELS} raster bands + {len(SCALAR_COLS)} scalars = {n_expected} "
        f"input channels, but the checkpoint was trained with {params.input_channels}. "
        "LAYER_PATHS or SCALAR_COLS differ from the training run."
    )
print(f"\n{N_SPATIAL_CHANNELS} raster bands + {len(SCALAR_COLS)} scalars = "
      f"{params.input_channels} input channels - matches the checkpoint")

title: deepSSF Inference
text:
ConvJointModel
The deepSSF model! A joint habitat–movement model with two heads: 1. Habitat head — a small CNN applied to the spatial window (env layers + tiled scalars) that outputs a per-pixel log-suitability map. 2. Movement head — a dense MLP (fully-connected layer) that takes the scalar covariates and the previous bearing, and produces parameters for a parametric movement kernel (a mixture of wrapped distributions centred on the current location).
The two log-probability surfaces are summed pixel-wise to give the joint predicted probability map for the animal’s next step.


Show code
model = deepssf.ConvJointModel(params).to(DEVICE)
n_params = sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters())
print(f"Model parameters : {n_params:,}")


Model parameters : 36,349

title: deepSSF Inference
text:
Load the trained model
ConvJointModel above is freshly initialised — random weights — so nothing it predicts means anything until a checkpoint is loaded into it. A training run writes three:

best_model.pt — the model to use for simulation. Both heads from one epoch, so the joint likelihood is the one that was actually measured.
best_model_habitat.pt / best_model_movement.pt — each head at its own best epoch, tracked across the whole run.

Mixing them is a deliberate trade: taking the habitat head from a different epoch gives the sharpest habitat surface to map, but the two heads then come from different epochs and the joint model’s likelihood is no longer what either checkpoint recorded. Use it for the landscape predictions below, not for simulating trajectories.
load_checkpoint() loads the weights in place and is strict about shapes, so a mismatch between the constants set above and the trained architecture raises here rather than silently predicting from a partly-random model.


Show code
# The joint model — used for all inference unless stated otherwise
ckpt = deepssf.load_checkpoint(str(CKPT_PATH), model)
print(f"best_model.pt          saved on '{ckpt['checkpoint_criterion']}' "
      f"= {ckpt['checkpoint_score']:.6f}")
print(f"                       trained with deepssf {ckpt.get('deepssf_version', 'unknown')}, "
      f"val_loss {ckpt['val_loss']:.6f}")

hab_ckpt = deepssf.load_checkpoint(str(OUTPUT_DIR / "best_model_habitat.pt"))
print(f"best_model_habitat.pt  saved on '{hab_ckpt['checkpoint_criterion']}' "
      f"= {hab_ckpt['checkpoint_score']:.6f}")
print(f"(a uniform surface over the window scores {np.log(WINDOW_SIZE ** 2):.4f})")

# Prediction only — no gradients needed, and this turns off dropout/batchnorm
# training behaviour.
model.eval()

# To map the sharpest habitat surface instead, overwrite just that head:
# load_head_weights(str(OUTPUT_DIR / "best_model_habitat.pt"), model, "habitat")

(a uniform surface over the window scores 7.8637)

  (scalar_grid_output): Scalar_to_Grid_Block()
  (conv_habitat): Conv2d_block_spatial(
    (conv2d): Sequential(
      (0): Conv2d(25, 8, kernel_size=(3, 3), stride=(1, 1), padding=(1, 1))
      (1): ReLU()
      (2): Conv2d(8, 8, kernel_size=(3, 3), stride=(1, 1), padding=(1, 1))
      (3): ReLU()
      (4): Conv2d(8, 8, kernel_size=(3, 3), stride=(1, 1), padding=(1, 1))
      (5): ReLU()
      (6): Conv2d(8, 8, kernel_size=(3, 3), stride=(1, 1), padding=(1, 1))
      (7): ReLU()
      (8): Conv2d(8, 8, kernel_size=(3, 3), stride=(1, 1), padding=(1, 1))

      (10): Conv2d(8, 8, kernel_size=(3, 3), stride=(1, 1), padding=(1, 1))

      (14): Conv2d(8, 1, kernel_size=(3, 3), stride=(1, 1), padding=(1, 1))
    )
  )

    (conv2d): Sequential(
      (0): Conv2d(25, 8, kernel_size=(3, 3), stride=(1, 1), padding=(1, 1))
      (1): ReLU()
      (2): MaxPool2d(kernel_size=2, stride=2, padding=0, dilation=1, ceil_mode=False)
      (3): Conv2d(8, 8, kernel_size=(3, 3), stride=(1, 1), padding=(1, 1))

section: Convert the NumPy rasters loaded earlier into PyTorch tensors
text:
Convert the NumPy rasters loaded earlier into PyTorch tensors
predict_habitat_landscape(), simulate_trajectory() and simulate_trajectories() all call get_landscape(month_index) to fetch the current environmental layers as a list of 2-D tensors.
With static (non-seasonal) rasters the month_index argument is unused. For seasonal data (e.g. monthly NDVI composites) you would index into a stack of layers here based on the current month.


Show code
# The simulation and prediction functions stack the list returned by
# get_landscape() along a new channel dimension, so every element must be a *2-D*
# tensor.  Unbind the band dimension of any multi-band layer so the channel order
# matches what MovementDataset fed the model during training.
landscape_tensors = []
for arr in env_layers.values():
    t = torch.from_numpy(np.asarray(arr).astype(np.float32))
    landscape_tensors.extend([t] if t.ndim == 2 else list(t))

print(f"Landscape channels: {len(landscape_tensors)}  (each {tuple(landscape_tensors[0].shape)})")


def get_landscape(_month_index):
    # Returns one 2-D tensor per spatial channel, in the same order as LAYER_PATHS.
    return landscape_tensors


Landscape channels: 12  (each (1335, 1715))

title: deepSSF Inference
text:
ScalarEncoder
Every question below is asked in natural units (“09:30 on day 200 at 33 °C”), but the model takes an encoded row in SCALAR_COLS order: the time of day and day of year as sin/cos pairs, the weather as z-scores (rain log-transformed first), wind direction as a sin/cos pair, and dt_hour as is. deepssf.ScalarEncoder does that conversion in both directions from a spec: one entry per natural-unit input saying how it maps to model columns.
The spec is specific to this model, so it is built here and saved next to the checkpoint (scalar_spec.json) for later stages and the app to load:

hour_t1 and yday_t1: cyclic, periods 24 h and 365.25 days (as in prepare_movement_df());
dt_hour: passed through unchanged;
the six weather covariates: linear, with the transform, mean and SD from scalar_scaling.csv;
wind direction: degrees to sin/cos, calm when the wind speed is 0, encoded as (0, 0). The data codes calm as direction 0 instead, but the two coincide (see the wind check above), and keying it on speed means a scenario cannot combine a wind speed with no direction.

The encoder also stores each input’s training range (from step_df), so a scenario outside the data the model saw gets a warning.


Show code
# Non-linear entries; the weather entries come from the training scaling table
SCALAR_SPEC = [
    {"type": "cyclic", "input": "hour_t1", "period": 24,
     "columns": ["hour_t1_sin1", "hour_t1_cos1"]},
    {"type": "cyclic", "input": "yday_t1", "period": 365.25,
     "columns": ["yday_t1_sin1", "yday_t1_cos1"]},
    {"type": "raw", "input": "dt_hour", "column": "dt_hour"},
    {"type": "circular_degrees", "input": WIND_DIR_COL,
     "columns": ["onpli_wind_dir_sin1", "onpli_wind_dir_cos1"],
     "calm": {"input": "onpli_wind_speed_kmh", "equals": 0}},
]

encoder = deepssf.ScalarEncoder.from_scaling_table(
    SCALING.loc[WEATHER_COLS],   # columns: transform, mean, sd; index: column
    SCALAR_COLS,
    extra_spec=SCALAR_SPEC,
    suffix="_scaled",
).ranges_from(step_df)          # training ranges of every input

SPEC_PATH = OUTPUT_DIR / "scalar_spec.json"
encoder.to_json(SPEC_PATH)
print(encoder)
print(f"Saved to {SPEC_PATH}\n")
print("Training ranges (natural units):")
print(pd.DataFrame(encoder.ranges, index=["min", "max"]).T.round(2).to_string())

title: deepSSF Inference
text:
HabitatLandscapePredictor
Partial dependence and the other summaries need habitat surfaces for many scalar scenarios over the same landscape. The scalars reach the habitat CNN only as constant channels in its first layer, so away from the padded edge their whole effect on that layer is one constant per output channel. deepssf.HabitatLandscapePredictor convolves the rasters with the first layer once, then, for each scenario, adds that constant and runs the remaining layers, batching scenarios together. It can also be restricted to a mask (for example, the area the pigs could reach; see the next section), which crops the work to the mask’s bounding box.

Check: identical to predict_habitat_landscape()
Three observed scenarios, compared on every cell outside the edge buffer, on the device. The two paths add the same numbers in a different order, so the differences should be float32 rounding (≪ 1e-4 in log-probability).


Show code
landscape = get_landscape(0)

t0 = time.perf_counter()
predictor = deepssf.HabitatLandscapePredictor(model, landscape, n_scalars=len(SCALAR_COLS))
setup_s = time.perf_counter() - t0
print(f"Predictor set up in {setup_s:.2f} s: {predictor.shape} cells, "
      f"{predictor.n_raster} raster channels, {predictor.edge_buffer}-px edge buffer, "
      f"{predictor.batch_size()} scenarios per batch by default")

check_scenarios = step_df.sample(3, random_state=7)
check_encoded = encoder.encode(check_scenarios)
fast = predictor.predict(check_encoded)

identity = []
for i, (step_idx, row) in enumerate(check_scenarios.iterrows()):
    ref = deepssf.predict_habitat_landscape(model, landscape, check_encoded[i])
    assert np.array_equal(np.isnan(ref), np.isnan(fast[i])), "valid cells differ"
    identity.append({
        "step": step_idx,
        "hour": row["hour_t1"],
        "yday": row["yday_t1"],
        "air_temp_c": row["onpli_air_temp_c"],
        "max_abs_diff": np.nanmax(np.abs(fast[i] - ref)),
        "fast_sum_p": np.nansum(np.exp(fast[i])),
    })
identity = pd.DataFrame(identity)
print(identity.to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda v: f"{v:.3g}"))
assert identity["max_abs_diff"].max() < 1e-4, "fast path differs from predict_habitat_landscape"
print(f"\nMax abs difference in log-probability: {identity['max_abs_diff'].max():.1e} (< 1e-4)")

Speed-up
Per scenario, and for a batch of 16 scenarios (the reference has to run them one at a time). Each timing is 3 warm-up runs then 5 timed runs on the device; results are returned to the CPU as NumPy arrays in both paths.


Show code
def time_runs(fn, n_warmup=3, n_timed=5):
    for _ in range(n_warmup):
        fn()
    times = []
    for _ in range(n_timed):
        t0 = time.perf_counter()
        fn()
        times.append(time.perf_counter() - t0)
    return np.array(times)


batch16 = encoder.encode(step_df.sample(16, random_state=11))
one = batch16[:1]

timings = {
    "reference, 1 scenario":
        time_runs(lambda: deepssf.predict_habitat_landscape(model, landscape, one[0])),
    "fast, 1 scenario":
        time_runs(lambda: predictor.predict(one)),
    "reference, 16 scenarios (loop)":
        time_runs(lambda: [deepssf.predict_habitat_landscape(model, landscape, s)
                           for s in batch16], n_warmup=1),
    f"fast, 16 scenarios (default batches of {predictor.batch_size()})":
        time_runs(lambda: predictor.predict(batch16)),
    "fast, 16 scenarios (one batch of 16)":
        time_runs(lambda: predictor.predict(batch16, batch_size=16)),
}
timing_table = pd.DataFrame({
    "mean_s": {k: v.mean() for k, v in timings.items()},
    "sd_s": {k: v.std(ddof=1) for k, v in timings.items()},
})
n_scen = np.array([1, 1, 16, 16, 16])
timing_table["per_scenario_s"] = timing_table["mean_s"] / n_scen
timing_table["speed_up"] = np.r_[
    [timing_table["mean_s"].iloc[0] / timing_table["mean_s"].iloc[i] for i in (0, 1)],
    [timing_table["mean_s"].iloc[2] / timing_table["mean_s"].iloc[i] for i in (2, 3, 4)],
]
print(f"Device: {DEVICE};  full landscape {predictor.shape}")
print(timing_table.round(4).to_string())

stage1_dir = INFERENCE_DIR / "stage1"
stage1_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
identity.to_csv(stage1_dir / "fast_path_identity.csv", index=False)
timing_table.assign(device=str(DEVICE)).to_csv(stage1_dir / "fast_path_timing.csv")

title: deepSSF Inference
section: Linked weather variables: dew point and wet bulb
text:
Linked weather variables: dew point and wet bulb
Air temperature, relative humidity (RH), dew point and wet bulb temperature are physically linked. Later sections change one at a time (e.g. temperature at a fixed dew point), and have to recompute the others to keep a scenario physically possible. The helpers in apps/weather_utils.py (shared with the app) use:

Dew point from temperature \(T\) and RH by the Magnus formula: \(\gamma = \ln(RH/100) + aT/(b+T)\), \(T_d = b\gamma/(a-\gamma)\), with \(a = 17.62\), \(b = 243.12\) °C (and its inverse for RH from \(T\) and \(T_d\)).
Wet bulb from \(T\) and RH by Stull (2011), which assumes sea-level pressure.

Both are checked against the station’s own dew point and wet bulb columns.


Show code
T_obs = step_df["onpli_air_temp_c"].to_numpy(float)
RH_obs = step_df["onpli_rel_humidity_pct"].to_numpy(float)
dew_obs = step_df["onpli_dew_point_temp_c"].to_numpy(float)
wet_obs = step_df["onpli_wet_bulb_temp_c"].to_numpy(float)

dew_est = wx.dew_point_c(T_obs, RH_obs)
wet_stull = wx.wet_bulb_stull_c(T_obs, RH_obs)


def error_summary(name, estimate, observed):
    err = estimate - observed
    return {
        "relation": name,
        "rmse_c": np.sqrt(np.mean(err**2)),
        "bias_c": err.mean(),
        "max_abs_c": np.abs(err).max(),
        "q01_c": np.quantile(err, 0.01),
        "q99_c": np.quantile(err, 0.99),
    }


psychro = [error_summary("dew point (Magnus)", dew_est, dew_obs),
           error_summary("wet bulb (Stull)", wet_stull, wet_obs)]

title: deepSSF Inference
text:
Availability mask
The habitat network only ever saw the 51 × 51-cell window around each fix, so the cells it has an opinion about for these pigs are the union of those windows: every cell within 25 cells (500 m) of an observed step’s start, in the Chebyshev (square-window) sense. deepssf.availability_mask() rasterises the fixes and dilates them with a max-pool. The fixes are the step starts the model was trained on (after the NA drop and the window filter).


Show code
MASK_RADIUS_PX = WINDOW_SIZE // 2
avail_mask = deepssf.availability_mask(
    landscape[0].shape, raster_transform, step_df["x1_"], step_df["y1_"], MASK_RADIUS_PX
)
print(f"Availability mask: {avail_mask.sum():,} of {avail_mask.size:,} cells "
      f"({avail_mask.mean():.1%} of the landscape), radius {MASK_RADIUS_PX} px "
      f"= {MASK_RADIUS_PX * PIXEL_SIZE:.0f} m")

# Class of the cell each step starts in
fix_cols, fix_rows = ~raster_transform * (step_df["x1_"].to_numpy(), step_df["y1_"].to_numpy())
fix_cols, fix_rows = np.floor(fix_cols).astype(int), np.floor(fix_rows).astype(int)
fix_class_idx = class_rasters[:, fix_rows, fix_cols].argmax(axis=0)
step_df["start_class"] = np.asarray(CLASS_NAMES)[fix_class_idx]

availability_table = pd.DataFrame({
    "class": CLASS_ORDER,
    "label": [CLASS_LABELS[c] for c in CLASS_ORDER],
    "landscape_share": [class_rasters[CLASS_NAMES.index(c)].mean() for c in CLASS_ORDER],
    "mask_share": [class_rasters[CLASS_NAMES.index(c)][avail_mask].mean() for c in CLASS_ORDER],
    "fix_share": [(step_df["start_class"] == c).mean() for c in CLASS_ORDER],
    "n_fixes": [(step_df["start_class"] == c).sum() for c in CLASS_ORDER],
})

title: deepSSF Inference
section: Habitat predictions restricted to the mask
text:
Habitat predictions restricted to the mask
From here on, surfaces come from a HabitatLandscapePredictor over the mask, and selection() turns natural-unit scenarios into log SR per class.


Show code
mask_predictor = deepssf.HabitatLandscapePredictor(
    model, landscape, n_scalars=len(SCALAR_COLS), mask=avail_mask
)
# Class rasters cropped to the predictor's grid, on the device, for class_selection
class_crop = torch.from_numpy(
    class_rasters[:, mask_predictor.row_slice, mask_predictor.col_slice]
).to(DEVICE)
print(f"Predictor grid {mask_predictor.shape} (bounding box of the mask + edge buffer), "
      f"{mask_predictor.valid.sum():,} valid cells, batches of {mask_predictor.batch_size()}")


def selection(natural_rows, scenario_ids=None):
    """Long DataFrame of use / availability / log SR per scenario and class."""
    encoded = encoder.encode(natural_rows)
    surfaces = mask_predictor.predict(encoded, as_numpy=False)
    return deepssf.class_selection(surfaces, class_crop, CLASS_NAMES,
                                   scenario_ids=scenario_ids)


def selection_wide(encoded, value="log_sr"):
    """Encoded rows [B, S] -> DataFrame [B, classes] of one class_selection column."""
    surfaces = mask_predictor.predict(encoded, as_numpy=False)
    df = deepssf.class_selection(surfaces, class_crop, CLASS_NAMES)
    return df.pivot(index="scenario", columns="class", values=value)[CLASS_NAMES]


Predictor grid (1122, 1501) (bounding box of the mask + edge buffer), 509,884 valid cells, batches of 6

title: deepSSF Inference
text:
Model vs empirical selection
A sanity check against the data. Empirically, use is the share of fixes in each class and availability is the class’s share of the mask. Model use is averaged over a fixed-seed sample of 500 observed steps’ own scalar inputs (time and weather), and log SR is computed from that average use.
The two are not expected to agree exactly. The habitat surface ranks every masked cell as if it were reachable, while real fixes are also shaped by movement (each fix is close to the previous one) and by where each pig’s home range is. But the ordering of the classes should match: dry rainforest selected, water and mudflat avoided.


Show code
N_EMPIRICAL_SCENARIOS = 500
empirical_sample = step_df.sample(N_EMPIRICAL_SCENARIOS, random_state=2026)
sample_sel = selection(empirical_sample, scenario_ids=empirical_sample.index)

mask_avail = availability_table.set_index("class")["mask_share"]
comparison = pd.DataFrame({
    "label": [CLASS_LABELS[c] for c in CLASS_ORDER],
    "availability": mask_avail.loc[CLASS_ORDER].to_numpy(),
    "empirical_use": availability_table.set_index("class").loc[CLASS_ORDER, "fix_share"].to_numpy(),
    "model_use": sample_sel.groupby("class")["use"].mean().loc[CLASS_ORDER].to_numpy(),
    "model_mean_log_sr": sample_sel.groupby("class")["log_sr"].mean().loc[CLASS_ORDER].to_numpy(),
}, index=pd.Index(CLASS_ORDER, name="class"))
with np.errstate(divide="ignore"):  # water has no fixes: log(0) = -inf, by design
    comparison["empirical_log_sr"] = np.log(comparison["empirical_use"] / comparison["availability"])
comparison["model_log_sr"] = np.log(comparison["model_use"] / comparison["availability"])
comparison.to_csv(STAGE2_DIR / "model_vs_empirical_log_sr.csv")
sample_sel.to_csv(STAGE2_DIR / "observed_scenarios_log_sr.csv", index=False)

       ylabel="Model log SR (habitat surface, mean over 500 observed scenarios)",
       title=f"Model vs empirical selection by class (r = {r:.2f}; water omitted)")

What this shows

The model ranks the classes much as the data do (r ≈ 0.8 across the nine classes plotted). Dry rainforest is the most strongly selected class in both, the melaleuca classes are selected, and mangrove is avoided. Water, left off the plot, is avoided by the model (log SR ≈ −1.4) and has no fixes.
The model is less extreme than the data. Dry rainforest’s empirical log SR (≈ 2.1) is far above the model’s (≈ 0.8). The share of fixes measures where pigs spend time, which includes long resting bouts in dense cover and is shaped by movement. The habitat surface ranks single cells as if all were reachable.
Mudflat is the exception. The pigs rarely use it (log SR ≈ −1.2), but the habitat surface is close to neutral on average and selects it in the daytime reference scenarios. Most masked mudflat is at the northern coastal margin; the joint model (habitat + movement) in the movement section is the place to check whether the next-step probabilities of entering it are lower.
There is a strong diel pattern in the reference scenarios. At 09:00 and 15:00 the eucalypt classes are avoided, and melaleuca woodland, mangrove and mudflat are selected. At night (03:00, 21:00) selection is much flatter. The partial dependence plots below separate this effect of the clock from the weather that comes with it.

print("Computing (or loading) 1-D partial dependence:")
pdp_results = {}
for name, spec in PDP_SPECS.items():
    base = spec.get("base", ice_base)
    grid = np.asarray(spec["grid"], dtype=float)
    pdp_results[name] = cached(
        f"pdp_{name}",
        {"grid": grid.tolist(), "base": base.index.tolist(), "set_fn": str(spec["set_fn"])},
        lambda: dict(zip(("pd", "ice"), deepssf.partial_dependence(
            log_sr_metric, base, spec["set_fn"], grid, encoder,
            batch_size=PD_BATCH, grid_name="value"))),
        n_maps=len(grid) * len(base),
    )

# Calm: wind direction is irrelevant when there is no wind
calm_result = cached(
    "pdp_wind_calm", {"base": ice_base_windy.index.tolist()},
    lambda: {"pd": log_sr_metric(encoder.encode(
        ice_base_windy.assign(onpli_wind_speed_kmh=0.0))).mean().rename("pd")
        .rename_axis("metric").reset_index()},

)

def class_grid(n=len(PLOT_CLASSES), ncols=3, height=2.4, width=3.6):
    nrows = int(np.ceil(n / ncols))
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(nrows, ncols, figsize=(width * ncols, height * nrows),
                             sharex=True, sharey=True, squeeze=False)
    return fig, axes.ravel()


def class_line(ax, x, y, cls, **kw):
    """A class-coloured line with a thin dark outline, so pale colours stay visible."""
    ax.plot(x, y, color=CLASS_COLOURS[cls], lw=2, zorder=4,
            path_effects=[pe.Stroke(linewidth=3.2, foreground="#4d4d4d"), pe.Normal()], **kw)


def plot_pdp(name, title):
    spec = PDP_SPECS[name]
    res = pdp_results[name]
    pd_df, ice_df = res["pd"], res["ice"]
    if name == "hour":  # close the daily cycle: 24:00 is 00:00
        pd_df = pd.concat([pd_df, pd_df[pd_df["value"] == 0].assign(value=24.0)])
        ice_df = pd.concat([ice_df, ice_df[ice_df["value"] == 0].assign(value=24.0)])
    fig, axes = class_grid()
    grid_vals = np.sort(pd_df["value"].unique())
    step = np.median(np.diff(grid_vals)) if len(grid_vals) > 1 else 1
    oor = pd_df.groupby("value")["frac_out_of_range"].first()
    rug = rug_sample[spec["rug"]].dropna().to_numpy()
    for ax, cls in zip(axes, PLOT_CLASSES):
        for v in oor.index[oor > 0.25]:
            ax.axvspan(v - step / 2, v + step / 2, color="#efefef", lw=0, zorder=0)
        ice = ice_df[ice_df["metric"] == cls]
        for _, curve in ice.groupby("ice_id"):
            ax.plot(curve["value"], curve["ice"], color="#9a9a9a", lw=0.5, alpha=0.35, zorder=2)
        sub = pd_df[pd_df["metric"] == cls]
        class_line(ax, sub["value"], sub["pd"], cls)
        ax.axhline(0, color="#555555", lw=0.7, zorder=3)
        ax.plot(rug, np.zeros_like(rug), "|", transform=ax.get_xaxis_transform(),
                color="#7a7a7a", ms=5, alpha=0.15, zorder=1)
        if name == "hour":
            for h in (SUNRISE_H, SUNSET_H):
                ax.axvline(h, color="#d08c00", lw=0.9, ls=":", zorder=3)
        if name == "wind_dir":
            ax.axhline(CALM_LOG_SR[cls], color=CLASS_COLOURS[cls], lw=1.2, ls="--", zorder=3,
                       path_effects=[pe.Stroke(linewidth=2.2, foreground="#4d4d4d"), pe.Normal()])
            ax.text(355, CALM_LOG_SR[cls], " calm", va="center", fontsize=7, color="#333333")
        ax.set_title(CLASS_LABELS[cls])
    for ax in axes[len(PLOT_CLASSES):]:
        ax.set_visible(False)
    for ax in axes[-3:]:
        ax.set_xlabel(spec["xlabel"])
    for ax in axes[::3]:
        ax.set_ylabel("log SR")
    extra = " Dotted lines: median sunrise and sunset." if name == "hour" else ""
    fig.suptitle(f"{title}\nPDP (coloured) and ICE curves (grey, one per base row); "
                 f"rug: observed values.{extra}", fontsize=10)
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig(STAGE3_DIR / f"pdp_{name}.png")
    plt.show()

section: Accumulated local effects of the thermal variables

Accumulated local effects of the thermal variables
Each variable is changed alone, but each row only across its own quantile bin, so the changes stay close to physically consistent weather. The curves are centred; read them as changes in log SR across the variable’s observed range.

title: deepSSF Inference
section: Observed-condition averages (M-plots), comparable to the empirical plots
text:
Observed-condition averages (M-plots), comparable to the empirical plots
The model’s log SR at 3,000 observed half-hours, averaged within bins of each variable. The bins follow bin_weather() in the empirical weather analysis: 10 quantile bins, a separate bin for zeros when more than 10 % of values are zero (rain, calm wind), and bins of 50 or fewer rows dropped. The hour plot uses 24 bins. These are not partial dependence plots: each bin carries the weather, season and time of day that came with it. The hour plot is the typical diel cycle, including the typical weather at each hour.

                        for i in range(0, len(mplot_rows), PD_BATCH)]),
        columns=CLASS_NAMES)},
    n_maps=len(mplot_rows),
)["log_sr"][CLASS_NAMES]

title: deepSSF Inference
text:
2-D partial dependence
How the diel pattern itself changes with heat stress, the season and rain. Each cell is the mean log SR over 20 base rows with both variables set. The colour scale is diverging and centred on 0 (blue = selected, red = avoided), and is shared across classes within a figure.


Show code

HOURS_2D = np.arange(0, 23, 2.0)

        ylabel="Day of year (mid-month)"),
    "hour_x_rain": dict(
        other="onpli_rain_30min_mm", values=[0, 0.4, 2, 8, 25],

        ylabel="Rain, 30 min (mm)"),

title: deepSSF Inference
text:
Interaction strength (Friedman’s H)
\(H^2\) is the share of the variance of the two-variable partial dependence that the two one-variable effects do not explain (0 = additive; values above ~0.2 are a substantial interaction). It is estimated from 20 base rows, so treat it as a rough ranking. H evaluates the partial dependence at the sample’s own values, and most half-hours are dry, so for hour × rain the sample is half raining and half dry rows (otherwise rain would barely vary in it).


Show code

    step_df[~raining].sample(N_H - N_H // 2, random_state=9),
])[encoder.inputs].assign(dt_hour=0.5)

    "hour × day of year": dict(var_b="yday_t1", set_fn_b=None, rows=h_base),
    "hour × rain": dict(var_b="onpli_rain_30min_mm", set_fn_b=None, rows=h_base_rain),
}
print("Computing (or loading) H statistics:")

What the partial dependence shows

Time matters more than weather. For every class, the day of year and the hour of day have the largest PDP ranges, about 0.7–2.5 log SR. The weather variables move selection by at most about 1 log SR, and most move it by much less. Permutation importance below checks this ranking for the model’s fit as a whole.
Diel cycle (the pure clock effect). Between about 08:00 and 14:00 the model selects dry rainforest, the melaleuca classes, mangrove and mudflat more strongly, and the two eucalypt classes less. At night the eucalypt classes are selected and the wetter classes avoided. The M-plot by hour (the typical diel cycle, weather included) has the same shape, so the daily cycle is not just an artefact of daytime heat.
Season. Floodplain sedgeland, mangrove and mudflat are selected in the dry season (mid-year) and strongly avoided in the wet season (January–March). The eucalypt classes are favoured in the wet season and avoided in the mid-dry season. Dry rainforest is most strongly selected around midday in the late dry season and build-up (September–November). The hour × day-of-year heatmaps show that the daily cycle itself changes with the season (H ≈ 0.2–0.45).
Heat stress. Moving temperature and humidity together towards a high wet bulb lowers selection of melaleuca closed forest, mangrove and mudflat (by ≈ 0.7–1.0 log SR over the observed range). It slightly raises melaleuca and eucalypt woodland, and leaves dry rainforest high. The ALE for wet bulb shows the same drop above ≈ 24 °C, using observed rows only.
Single thermal variables need care. The ALEs for dew point and RH run partly opposite to wet bulb: the model’s four correlated thermal inputs offset each other, so no one of them should be read alone. The consistent axes (temperature at fixed dew point, RH at fixed temperature, heat stress) are the interpretable ones.
M-plots vs PDPs. The observed-condition averages show much steeper declines of mangrove, mudflat and floodplain at high dew point or RH than the PDPs do. That is mostly the wet season showing through, because humid conditions occur in the wet season. This is why the M-plots match the empirical binned plots but should not be read as weather effects.
Rain and wind have small effects, except that heavy rain raises mangrove and water selection. Heavy rain is rare, so those ICE curves rest on few observations.

title: deepSSF Inference
section: Which variables move each class’s selection most?
text:
Which variables move each class’s selection most?
A cheap, class-specific complement: the standard deviation of each class’s 1-D partial dependence curve from the previous section (in-range grid values only). A flat curve means the variable barely changes how strongly the class is selected. The grids differ between variables, so compare the shading within a column more than across columns.


Show code
pdp_var = (in_range.groupby(["class", "variable"])["pd"].std()
           .unstack("variable").loc[PLOT_CLASSES, list(PDP_SPECS)])
pdp_var.to_csv(STAGE4_DIR / "pdp_sd_importance.csv")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9.5, 4.8))
im = ax.imshow(pdp_var.to_numpy(), cmap="Blues", aspect="auto", vmin=0)
ax.set_xticks(range(pdp_var.shape[1]), [c.replace("_", " ") for c in pdp_var.columns],
              rotation=30, ha="right")
ax.set_yticks(range(pdp_var.shape[0]), [CLASS_LABELS[c] for c in pdp_var.index])
vmax = pdp_var.to_numpy().max()
for i in range(pdp_var.shape[0]):
    for j in range(pdp_var.shape[1]):
        v = pdp_var.iat[i, j]
        ax.text(j, i, f"{v:.2f}", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=7,
                color="white" if v > 0.6 * vmax else "#222222")
ax.grid(False)
fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax, label="SD of the PDP (log SR)")
ax.set_title("PDP-variance importance: how much each variable moves each class's selection",
             fontsize=10)
fig.tight_layout()
fig.savefig(STAGE4_DIR / "pdp_sd_importance.png")
plt.show()










What the importance shows

Landcover is what the model relies on most (+0.11 nats per step in the joint NLL when shuffled), followed by time of day and day of year (≈ +0.08 each). The thermal group adds +0.02, DEM +0.01, wind and slope +0.005, and rain and dt_hour almost nothing. The baseline joint NLL on the sample (4.01) matches the checkpoint’s validation loss.
The two heads use time differently. The habitat surface depends on day of year (+0.14) far more than on time of day (+0.03). The movement kernel depends most on time of day (+0.06), then day of year (+0.05) and landcover (+0.04). The daily cycle acts mainly through how far pigs move; the seasonal cycle acts through where they go.
Weather acts mostly through movement. The thermal and wind groups have small positive importance for the movement and joint NLL, and slightly negative values for the habitat head on its own. The model was trained on the joint likelihood, so the habitat head’s stand-alone NLL is not what was optimised. The negative values mean only that these inputs don’t improve the habitat surface’s own fit.
Individually, the cosine of the hour (night vs day) and both day-of-year terms dominate. Among the thermal inputs, air temperature, RH and dew point each add about +0.01, a share of the group’s total, as expected for correlated inputs.
The rankings are stable: the SD over permutations is about 5 % of each increase.
By class (the heatmap above): day of year moves selection of mangrove, mudflat and floodplain the most; hour moves mangrove, mudflat and the melaleuca classes; heat stress is the most influential weather axis for mudflat, melaleuca closed forest and mangrove.

section: Calibration: does the kernel match the observed steps?
text:
Calibration: does the kernel match the observed steps?
Checked on a fixed sample of 5,000 observed steps before interpreting anything else:

Step length by hour. The model’s expected step length (movement-only and joint), averaged over the steps in each hour, against the observed mean and median step length (sl_). The model’s median is the median of the steps’ pooled distance distributions.
Randomised PIT of the observed step lengths. For each step, take the kernel’s probability of a shorter step plus a uniform random share of the probability at exactly the observed cell distance. If the kernel’s step-length distribution is right, these values are uniform on [0, 1]. A U-shape means the kernel is too narrow; a hump means it is too wide; a slope means a bias.
Next-step landcover. The joint kernel’s average probability of each class for the next step, against the observed share of next steps in each class.

                          "pmf_joint": pd.DataFrame(t_p[1]["joint"]),

section: Movement partial dependence by starting class
text:
Movement partial dependence by starting class
For 60 observed windows per starting class, one scalar input is changed at a time (linked weather variables change consistently, as for habitat), and the movement kernel is summarised. Lines are the mean over the 60 windows (the PDP); bands are their interquartile range (the spread of the ICE curves). dt_hour = 0.5 h.


Show code
N_MOVE_BASE = 60
move_base = pd.concat([
    d.sample(N_MOVE_BASE, random_state=12)
    for _, d in step_df.dropna(subset=["start_group"]).groupby("start_group")
])
move_base_natural = move_base[encoder.inputs].assign(dt_hour=0.5)

    "hour": ("hour_t1", np.arange(0, 24, 1.0), "Hour of day"),
    "yday": ("yday_t1", MONTH_MID_DAYS, "Day of year"),
    "rain": ("onpli_rain_30min_mm", [0, 0.4, 2, 8, 25], "Rain, 30 min (mm)"),
    "wind_speed": ("onpli_wind_speed_kmh", [0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30], "Wind speed (km/h)"),
    "air_temp_fixed_dew": (set_air_temp, np.arange(15, 39.1, 3), "Air temp. (°C), fixed dew point"),
    "rh_fixed_temp": (set_rh, np.arange(20, 96, 10), "RH (%), fixed temperature"),
    "heat_stress": (set_heat_stress, np.arange(14, 29.1, 1.5), "Heat stress: wet bulb (°C)"),
}


def movement_pdp(set_fn, grid):
    setter = (lambda r, v: r.assign(**{set_fn: v})) if isinstance(set_fn, str) else set_fn
    frames = []
    for v in grid:
        tab = kernel_table(move_base, natural=setter(move_base_natural, v), with_classes=True)
        frames.append(tab.assign(value=v, start_group=move_base["start_group"].to_numpy())
                      .reset_index(names="step"))
    return pd.concat(frames, ignore_index=True)

section: Where does the next step go?
text:
Where does the next step go?
The joint kernel’s probability that the next step lands in each landcover class, against the hour of day and heat stress, for each starting class (the same 60 windows per class). This combines where the pig could go (movement) with where it prefers to go (habitat), within the classes actually around it.


Show code
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, len(START_GROUPS), figsize=(17, 6.5), sharey="row")
for row, name in enumerate(["hour", "heat_stress"]):

                    path_effects=[pe.Stroke(linewidth=3, foreground="#4d4d4d"), pe.Normal()])
        ax.set(xlabel=MOVE_PDP_SPECS[name][2])
        if row == 0:
            ax.set_title(f"Starting in {group}")

handles = {}
for ax in axes.ravel():

        handles.setdefault(lab, hnd)

title: deepSSF Inference
section: Example kernels: floodplain, cool morning vs hot afternoon
text:
Example kernels: floodplain, cool morning vs hot afternoon
One observed window starting in floodplain sedgeland, with two scenarios: 06:00 in cool, dry weather (wet bulb 18 °C) and 15:00 in hot, humid weather (wet bulb 27.5 °C), each with the typical temperature and humidity for that wet bulb. The first four columns show the window’s landcover and the habitat, movement and joint surfaces (log-probability; north up; the habitat and joint surfaces leave out the padded edge cells). The last column compares the joint and movement kernels’ step-length densities (exact, from the grid) with the observed step lengths of floodplain steps in similar conditions (±2 h, ±1.5 °C wet bulb).


Show code
flood = step_df[step_df["start_class"] == "veg_floodplain_sedgeland"]
# A window with mixed landcover around it (at least 3 classes covering 5 %+)
flood_sample = flood.sample(400, random_state=13)
cw = deepssf.crop_windows(class_dev, flood_sample["x1_"], flood_sample["y1_"], raster_transform,
                          WINDOW_SIZE).clamp_min(0).mean(dim=(2, 3)).cpu().numpy()
example = flood_sample.iloc[int(np.argmax((cw > 0.05).sum(axis=1)))]
example_df = example.to_frame().T
EXAMPLES = {"06:00, cool & dry (wet bulb 18 °C)": (6.0, 18.0),
            "15:00, hot & humid (wet bulb 27.5 °C)": (15.0, 27.5)}

ex_spatial = deepssf.crop_windows(landscape_dev, example_df["x1_"], example_df["y1_"],
                                  raster_transform, WINDOW_SIZE)
ex_classes = deepssf.crop_windows(class_dev, example_df["x1_"], example_df["y1_"],
                                  raster_transform, WINDOW_SIZE)[0].cpu().numpy()
ex_bearing = torch.tensor([[float(example["bearing_tm1"])]], device=DEVICE)
bins = np.arange(0, 520, 25)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 5, figsize=(17, 6.6))
for row, (title, (hour, wb)) in enumerate(EXAMPLES.items()):
    nat = set_heat_stress(example_df[encoder.inputs].assign(dt_hour=0.5, hour_t1=hour,
                                                            onpli_rain_30min_mm=0.0), wb)
    scal = torch.from_numpy(encoder.encode(nat)).to(DEVICE)
    surf = deepssf.next_step_surfaces(model, ex_spatial, scal, ex_bearing, edge_buffer=EDGE)
    hab, move, joint = surf["habitat"][0], surf["movement"][0], surf["joint"][0]
    panels = [("Habitat", hab), ("Movement", move), ("Joint (next step)", joint)]
    lc = np.where(ex_classes.max(axis=0) > 0, ex_classes.argmax(axis=0), -1)
    axes[row, 0].imshow(np.ma.masked_less(lc, 0), cmap=landcover_cmap, vmin=-0.5,
                        vmax=len(CLASS_NAMES) - 0.5, interpolation="nearest")
    axes[row, 0].set_title("Landcover" if row == 0 else "")
    axes[row, 0].set_ylabel(title, fontsize=9)
    for ax, (name, surf) in zip(axes[row, 1:4], panels):
        s = surf.cpu().numpy()
        s = np.where(np.isfinite(s), s, np.nan)  # excluded edge cells: blank
        ax.imshow(s, cmap="viridis", vmin=np.nanpercentile(s, 5), vmax=np.nanmax(s),
                  interpolation="nearest")
        ax.set_title(name if row == 0 else "")
    for ax in axes[row, :4]:
        ax.plot(HALF, HALF, marker="+", color="white", ms=8, mew=1.5)
        ax.set_xticks([]), ax.set_yticks([])
        ax.grid(False)
    # Step-length densities from the grid, vs observed steps in similar conditions
    ax = axes[row, 4]
    for name, kern, colour in (("joint", joint, "#2b6cb0"), ("movement", move, "#c05621")):
        p = torch.softmax(kern.reshape(-1), dim=0)
        pmf = torch.zeros(len(UNIQUE_D), device=DEVICE).index_add_(0, D_INDEX, p).cpu().numpy()
        dens = np.histogram(unique_d, bins=bins, weights=pmf)[0] / np.diff(bins)
        ax.stairs(dens, bins, color=colour, lw=1.8, label=f"model ({name})")
    hour_diff = (flood["hour_t1"] - hour + 12) % 24 - 12
    similar = flood[(hour_diff.abs() <= 2) & ((flood["onpli_wet_bulb_temp_c"] - wb).abs() <= 1.5)]
    ax.hist(similar["sl_"], bins=bins, density=True, color="#bbbbbb", label=f"observed (n={len(similar)})")
    ax.set(xlabel="Step length (m)", ylabel="Density", yscale="log")
    ax.legend(loc="upper right")

             fontsize=10)
fig.tight_layout()

Dry Rainforest        38.0  25.0  13.0        14.0                18.0            2.0          9.0
Eucalypt Open Forest  65.0  47.0  20.0        25.0                16.0            2.0          6.0
Eucalypt Woodland     50.0  40.0  12.0        25.0                11.0            5.0          5.0
