Melaleuca (pooled)    38.0  24.0  15.0        10.0                28.0            5.0         13.0



What the movement kernel shows
Calibration first. - The model’s mean step length by hour follows the observed diel cycle: a dawn peak (observed ≈ 90 m at 05:00–07:00) and a midday low (≈ 40 m). Overall, the movement kernel alone gives 68 m and the joint kernel 57 m, against 61 m observed. The joint kernel leaves out the habitat surface’s padded edge cells, so it cannot place a step more than 340 m out along either axis. 2 % of observed steps go that far, which is why it sits a little low, most of all at the dawn peak (≈ 80 m vs 91 m). - The model’s pooled median moves in grid steps (20, 28, 40 m) and sits a little above the observed median, so very short steps are slightly under-predicted. - The PIT histograms have a mild central hump (central deciles 0.12–0.135 vs the uniform 0.10), so the kernel is a little too wide. The joint PIT’s top decile (0.11) is raised by the same 2 % of long steps. - Next-step landcover is very well calibrated. The joint kernel’s predicted shares match the observed next-step classes to within about 0.5 percentage points for every class, e.g. mudflat 1.9 % predicted vs 1.7 % observed. So the habitat surface’s apparent liking for mudflat at the landscape scale (in the landcover selection section) does not carry through to predicted steps once movement is included.
Grid vs untruncated kernel. The decoded gamma mixture has a mean of about 30 m, but the grid kernel’s expected step is about 68 m, and the window truncates almost nothing (outer-ring mass 0.002). The difference is discretisation. The fitted gamma puts much of its mass within 10 m (inside the centre cell), but the grid evaluates the density only at cell centres (7.6 m for the centre cell, 20 m for its neighbours) and then renormalises, which moves that mass outwards. The model was fitted, and is used, on the grid, so the grid summaries are the ones to interpret; the decoded gamma parameters are not step-length distributions in their own right.
Effects on movement. - Hour is by far the strongest. Expected steps peak at dawn (05:00–07:00) and are shortest around midday, for every starting class: a range of 26 m (floodplain) to 65 m (eucalypt open forest). P(stay) is lowest at dawn (≈ 0.21) and highest at midday (≈ 0.33). Directional persistence is weak throughout (turning resultant < 0.1) and is highest at dawn. - Season: steps are longest in the build-up and early wet season (October–December) and shortest mid-dry season (around July). - Weather effects are modest: - stronger wind shortens steps (by 10–25 m from calm to 30 km/h); - heavy rain shortens them a little; - higher temperature at a fixed dew point shortens steps from melaleuca and dry rainforest (by up to ≈ 28 m); - humidity and the heat-stress axis change expected steps by less than 15 m. - The starting class matters as much as the conditions. Pigs starting in eucalypt open forest or woodland take the longest steps, and those on the floodplain the shortest. - Where the next step goes: pigs mostly stay in the class they are in (P ≈ 0.75–0.93). The exception is the pooled melaleuca classes, which are interleaved with each other and with dry rainforest. Moves from eucalypt woodland into eucalypt open forest, and from floodplain into melaleuca, peak around dawn, when steps are longest.

text:
load_environmental_layers()
Reads each GeoTIFF listed in LAYER_PATHS, min–max

Scales every band to [0, 1], and returns:

env_layers — dict mapping layer name → NumPy array: 2-D (H × W) for single-band GeoTIFFs, 3-D (bands × H × W) for multi-band ones, where each band becomes its own model input channel
raster_transform — Affine object that converts pixel (row, col) indices to the projected coordinates (easting, northing) of the raster(s), which should be in the same CRS as the GPS data. This transform is used whenever we need to translate between pixel space and real-world coordinates.


Two things to watch for:

The keys 's2' and 's2_dir' are reserved for the monthly Sentinel-2 composite loader — a single GeoTIFF passed under the name 's2' is silently skipped (see the note in the paths cell above).
The rescaling uses a single global min/max across all bands of a file, and computes (data - lo) / hi rather than (data - lo) / (hi - lo). Our index raster is int16 scaled by 10 000 with ±10 000 fill values, so the loaded values span [0, 2] rather than [0, 1] and the three indices are not individually normalised. That is workable (the CNN can rescale internally) but if it hurts training, pre-scale each band yourself and save as .npy — non-.tif paths in LAYER_PATHS are loaded with np.load(..., mmap_mode='r') and left untouched, though at least one real .tif must remain in the dict so the transform can be set.

N_SPATIAL_CHANNELS = sum(1 if arr.ndim == 2 else arr.shape[0] for arr in env_layers.values())

title: deepSSF Model Training
text:
SCALAR_COLS
These are non-spatial inputs. For processing with convolutional layers, they are converted into spatial windows (rasters/arrays), and stacked with the truly spatial covariates.
The model receives a fixed-size spatial window centred on each step’s start location. To let the network express time-varying habitat preferences (e.g. different nocturnal vs diurnal use), scalar covariates are tiled into additional channels of the same H × W size, so every pixel “knows” the current time context when habitat suitability is estimated.

hour_t1_sin1 / hour_t1_cos1

Sine and cosine of (2π × hour / 24), encoding time-of-day as a circular variable. The circular encoding means 23:00 and 01:00 are treated as adjacent — a plain hour value would have an artificial discontinuity at midnight.

yday_t1_sin1 / yday_t1_cos1

Same circular encoding for day-of-year (1–365), capturing seasonal variation in habitat use (e.g. dry-season vs wet-season movements).

dt_hour

Elapsed time between consecutive fixes (hours). Because GPS collars do not always fix at a perfectly regular rate, including dt_hour lets the movement kernel rescale expected displacement proportionally to the actual time interval rather than assuming a fixed fix rate. Note: dt_hour must be supplied at simulation time as well, so that simulate_trajectory() produces inputs consistent with training.

Weather covariates from the onpli_ weather station, carried over from the CSV for the start of each step:

rain_30min_mm, air_temp_c, wet_bulb_temp_c, dew_point_temp_c, rel_humidity_pct, wind_speed_kmh

Standardised to z-scores (the *_scaled columns) before going into the model, with rain log-transformed, log(1 + x), first. The mean and SD are kept so model inputs and effects can be converted back to natural units.

wind_dir_deg

Encoded as a sine/cosine pair (onpli_wind_dir_sin1 / onpli_wind_dir_cos1) for the same wraparound reason as hour of day, with calm steps set to (0, 0).





Show code
# Time covariates derived by prepare_movement_df().  Not scaled: the sin/cos pairs
# are already in [-1, 1], and simulate_trajectory() fills dt_hour with the raw
# time_between_steps (hours), so the model has to be trained on raw hours too.
TIME_COLS = ["hour_t1_sin1",
             "hour_t1_cos1",
             "yday_t1_sin1",
             "yday_t1_cos1",
             "dt_hour"]

# Weather covariates carried over from the CSV in natural units, and standardised
# to z-scores further down (the "_scaled" columns)
WEATHER_COLS = ["onpli_rain_30min_mm",
                "onpli_air_temp_c",
                "onpli_wet_bulb_temp_c",
                "onpli_dew_point_temp_c",
                "onpli_rel_humidity_pct",
                "onpli_wind_speed_kmh"
                ]

# Wind direction (degrees) is carried over, then encoded as a sin/cos pair further
# down rather than scaled
WIND_DIR_COL = "onpli_wind_dir_deg"

# The model inputs, in the order the model sees them
SCALAR_COLS = (
    TIME_COLS
    + [f"{col}_scaled" for col in WEATHER_COLS]
    + ["onpli_wind_dir_sin1", "onpli_wind_dir_cos1"]
)
print(f"{len(SCALAR_COLS)} scalar inputs: {SCALAR_COLS}")

title: deepSSF Model Training
text:
prepare_movement_df()
Converts a fixes dataframe (one row per GPS location) into a step dataframe (one row per movement between consecutive fixes).

For each step it computes:

dx, dy — displacement in projected CRS units (metres)
bearing — direction of travel (radians; 0 = north, clockwise positive)
bearing_tm1 — bearing of the previous step, used as a model input so the network can capture directional persistence by estimating a turning angle
dt_hour — time elapsed between consecutive fixes (hours)
hour_t1, yday_t1 — decimal hour-of-day and day-of-year at the step start location
*_sin1 / *_cos1 — sine/cosine encodings of hour and yday (see SCALAR_COLS below)


The “1” on column names (x1_, y1_, t1_, etc.) flags them as “start of step” variables; and the “2” in x2_, y2_, t2_ are the corresponding “end of step” values, following the convention of the amt package (Signer et al. 2019). The last fix for each individual is dropped because no forward step can be formed.


Show code
# The CSV is already in amt step format, but prepare_movement_df() expects one row
# per *fix* and rebuilds the steps itself (it also derives bearing, dt_hour and the
# cyclic time encodings the model needs).  Point it at the step-start columns and
# let it re-form the steps from consecutive fixes.
step_df = deepssf.prepare_movement_df(
    raw_df, 
    id_col="name", 
    time_col="t1_", 
    x_col="x1_", 
    y_col="y1_",
    # derives the time cols; carries the weather and wind direction cols over
    scalar_cols=TIME_COLS + WEATHER_COLS + [WIND_DIR_COL],
)
n_dropped = len(raw_df) - len(step_df)
print(f"Movement steps : {len(step_df):,}  ({n_dropped} dropped — last per individual)")

Encode wind direction as a sin/cos pair
Wind direction follows the BoM convention: the compass bearing the wind blows from, in 10° steps clockwise from north (90 = from the east). North is recorded as 360, and 0 is reserved for calm (no wind, so no direction).
Taking the sine and cosine removes the wraparound, so 350° and 10° sit next to each other and 0° and 360° both mean north: - onpli_wind_dir_sin1 — east–west component (+1 = from the east, −1 = from the west) - onpli_wind_dir_cos1 — north–south component (+1 = from the north, −1 = from the south)
Calm steps are set to (0, 0). A plain sin/cos of 0° gives (0, 1), which the model would read as a northerly. wind_dir_from_sin_cos() converts back to 0–360° (0 = north), returning NaN for calm.


Show code
def wind_dir_to_sin_cos(deg):
    """Compass degrees (0 = north, clockwise) -> (sin, cos)."""
    rad = np.radians(np.asarray(deg, dtype=float))
    return np.sin(rad), np.cos(rad)


def wind_dir_from_sin_cos(sin1, cos1):
    """(sin, cos) -> compass degrees in [0, 360), 0 = north.  NaN for calm (0, 0)."""
    sin1 = np.asarray(sin1, dtype=float)
    cos1 = np.asarray(cos1, dtype=float)
    # Round before wrapping so north comes back as 0 rather than 359.99999...
    deg = np.round(np.degrees(np.arctan2(sin1, cos1)), 6) % 360
    return np.where(np.hypot(sin1, cos1) < 1e-6, np.nan, deg)

Standardise the weather covariates
Converts each weather covariate to a z-score, (x − mean) / SD, so it sits on a similar scale to the sin/cos time encodings. The natural-unit columns stay in step_df, and the scaled copies get a _scaled suffix.
Rain is mostly 0 with a long tail of heavy falls, so on its own a z-score would put the biggest downpours dozens of SDs out. Rain is therefore log-transformed first, log(1 + x), which keeps 0 at 0 and pulls in the tail, and the z-score is taken on the logged values.
The transform, mean and SD for each column are stored in SCALING and saved to scalar_scaling.csv in OUTPUT_DIR: - unscale_covariate(values, col) converts back to natural units: natural = scaled × SD + mean, followed by exp(x) − 1 for log1p columns. - scale_covariate(values, col) scales new weather values, e.g. for prediction or simulation, with these same coefficients. - To reload them later: pd.read_csv(OUTPUT_DIR / "scalar_scaling.csv", index_col="column"). The two functions only read SCALING, so they work on the reloaded table.


Show code
# Columns log-transformed, log(1 + x), before the z-score.  Add any other heavily
# right-skewed, non-negative covariates here.
LOG1P_COLS = ["onpli_rain_30min_mm"]

# Transform, mean and SD for each weather covariate (after dropping NAs).  The
# mean/SD are of the transformed values, i.e. of log(1 + rain) for rain.
SCALING = pd.DataFrame(
    {"transform": ["log1p" if col in LOG1P_COLS else "none" for col in WEATHER_COLS]},
    index=pd.Index(WEATHER_COLS, name="column"),
)
for col in WEATHER_COLS:
    values = step_df[col].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    if SCALING.at[col, "transform"] == "log1p":
        values = np.log1p(values)
    SCALING.at[col, "mean"] = values.mean()
    SCALING.at[col, "sd"] = values.std(ddof=1)


def scale_covariate(values, col):
    """Natural units -> model scale for `col`: log1p if listed, then z-score."""
    values = np.asarray(values, dtype=float)
    if SCALING.at[col, "transform"] == "log1p":
        values = np.log1p(values)
    return (values - SCALING.at[col, "mean"]) / SCALING.at[col, "sd"]


def unscale_covariate(values, col):
    """Model scale -> natural units for `col`: undo the z-score, then expm1 if logged."""
    values = np.asarray(values, dtype=float) * SCALING.at[col, "sd"] + SCALING.at[col, "mean"]
    if SCALING.at[col, "transform"] == "log1p":
        values = np.expm1(values)
    return values


for col in WEATHER_COLS:
    step_df[f"{col}_scaled"] = scale_covariate(step_df[col], col)

SCALING.to_csv(OUTPUT_DIR / "scalar_scaling.csv")
print("Scaling coefficients:")
print(SCALING.round(3).to_string())

           for col in WEATHER_COLS)

title: deepSSF Model Training
text:
PIXEL_SIZE
Raster resolution in CRS units (metres here). Read straight off raster_transform rather than typed in: the transform is the authority on the grid the model is trained against, and a hand-entered value that disagrees with it silently mis-scales the movement kernel — which is parameterised in metres — against a grid measured in pixels.


Show code
# transform.a is the cell width, transform.e the (negative) cell height
PIXEL_SIZE = abs(raster_transform.a)

if not math.isclose(abs(raster_transform.a), abs(raster_transform.e)):
    raise ValueError(
        f"Non-square pixels ({abs(raster_transform.a)} x {abs(raster_transform.e)}); "
        "the model assumes square cells."
    )

WINDOW_SIZE
The size of the local availability window in cells/pixels.
The maximum step length that the model will allow is the distance between the centre cell and the nearest edge (in reality some steps may be longer if they are in the corners).

title: deepSSF Model Training
text:
BATCH_SIZE
Number of training samples (movement steps) per training mini-batch


Show code
BATCH_SIZE  = 128

title: deepSSF Model Training
text:
N_CONV_LAYERS_MOVE
How many convolutional layers in the movement subnetwork of the model?
Each of the convolution layers has a max pooling layer, so more layers will result in greater dimension reduction that will feed into the fully-connected layer that outputs the movement parameters.


Show code
N_CONV_LAYERS_MOVE = 4

title: deepSSF Model Training
text:
N_CONV_LAYERS_HAB
How many convolutional layers in the habitat selection subnetwork of the model?
These convolution layers do not have max pooling layers, so there is no dimension reduction. More layers will increase the depth of the model and allow for more abstracted features to be identified, but will slow model training/prediction.
This count includes the final convolution layer, which is the one that collapses the feature maps down to the single-channel habitat selection surface, so the minimum is 1.


Show code
N_CONV_LAYERS_HAB = 4

title: deepSSF Model Training
text:
OUTPUT_CHANNELS
Number of convolutional filters (and therefore feature maps) for each convolution layer. More convolutional filters can provide more flexible functions, but will increase the number of parameters and slow down training times.


Show code
OUTPUT_CHANNELS = 8

title: deepSSF Model Training
text:
DENSE_DIM_HIDDEN
How many neurons are in each layer of the multilayer perceptron for the movement subnetwork, after the convolution layers?


Show code
DENSE_DIM_HIDDEN = 128



Pre-calculate the flattened CNN output size
This value will be the input to the fully-connected layers in the movement subnetwork, and is calculated here so that ModelParams can be set without hard-coding it.
flattened_conv_dim() reproduces exactly what the layers inside ConvJointModel do to the spatial dimensions: * conv (padding=1) keeps the spatial dimension unchanged at each layer * maxpool k=2, s=2 halves the spatial dimension (floor division) at each layer
Because every movement conv layer is paired with a max pooling layer, this size depends on N_CONV_LAYERS_MOVE — so it has to be recalculated whenever that (or WINDOW_SIZE, or OUTPUT_CHANNELS) changes. It raises an error if the window is pooled away to nothing, which means too many layers for the window size.


Show code
DENSE_DIM = deepssf.flattened_conv_dim(
    image_dim=WINDOW_SIZE,
    n_conv_layers_move=N_CONV_LAYERS_MOVE,
    output_channels=OUTPUT_CHANNELS,
)
print(f"After {N_CONV_LAYERS_MOVE}x conv+maxpool: dense_dim_in_all={DENSE_DIM}")


After 4x conv+maxpool: dense_dim_in_all=72

title: deepSSF Model Training
text:
make_dataloaders()
Splits step_df into train / val / test subsets (here 80 / 10 / 10 %) and returns a PyTorch DataLoader for each.
The split is a torch.utils.data.random_split, not a chronological one — each subset is a random sample of steps drawn from across the whole dataset and all 28 individuals. Consecutive steps are highly autocorrelated, so a random split leaks information between train and test and will make the validation numbers below look better than genuine out-of-sample performance. If you want an honest held-out estimate, split step_df yourself (by individual, or by time) and build the DataLoaders from the resulting subsets.

Each DataLoader yields tuples of:

x1 — spatial window tensor (batch × n_spatial_channels × H × W)

One channel per raster band in LAYER_PATHS, cropped around each step’s start pixel.

x2 — scalar covariate tensor (batch × len(SCALAR_COLS))

Raw scalar values; broadcast into spatial maps inside the model.

x3 — previous bearing tensor (batch × 1)

Conditions the movement kernel on the direction of the prior step.

(px2, py2) — pixel indices of the true next location within the window

Used by the loss function to look up the predicted probability at the observed destination.



The layer_paths argument causes the function to re-read the rasters internally, so the DataLoader is independent of the env_layers dict loaded above.


Show code
dl_train, dl_val, dl_test = deepssf.make_dataloaders(
    layer_paths=LAYER_PATHS,
    window_size=WINDOW_SIZE,
    batch_size=BATCH_SIZE,
    train_split=0.8,
    val_split=0.1,
    scalar_cols=SCALAR_COLS,
    df=step_df,
)

title: deepSSF Model Training
text:
ModelParams
A thin dict-like container (it is a wrapper around something else rather than storing data) that groups all architecture hyper-parameters so they can be passed to ConvJointModel and logged together.
This is where the parameters that are passed to the model are set.


Show code
params = deepssf.ModelParams({
    "batch_size":                BATCH_SIZE,
    "image_dim":                 WINDOW_SIZE,           # spatial window size (pixels)
    "pixel_size":                PIXEL_SIZE,            # metres per pixel
    "dim_in_nonspatial_to_grid": len(SCALAR_COLS),      # scalar cols tiled into window
    "dense_dim_in_nonspatial":   len(SCALAR_COLS),      # scalar inputs to the dense MLP
    "dense_dim_hidden":          DENSE_DIM_HIDDEN,      # hidden units in the movement MLP
    "dense_dim_in_all":          DENSE_DIM,             # flattened CNN output size
    # One channel per raster band (not per layer) + the tiled scalar covariates
    "input_channels":            N_SPATIAL_CHANNELS + len(SCALAR_COLS),
    "output_channels":           OUTPUT_CHANNELS,       # feature maps per conv layer
    "kernel_size":               3,                     # conv kernel spatial size
    "stride":                    1,                     # conv stride (should be kept at 1)
    "kernel_size_mp":            2,                     # max-pool kernel size
    "stride_mp":                 2,                     # max-pool stride 
    "padding":                   1,                     # same-padding preserves spatial dimensions
    "num_movement_params":       12,                    # movement kernel parameters
    "n_conv_layers_hab":         N_CONV_LAYERS_HAB,     # conv layers, habitat branch
    "n_conv_layers_move":        N_CONV_LAYERS_MOVE,    # conv+maxpool layers, movement
    "dropout":                   0.0,
    "device":                    DEVICE,
})
print(f"input_channels: {params.input_channels}  (must match x1 channels + len(SCALAR_COLS))")


input_channels: 25  (must match x1 channels + len(SCALAR_COLS))

title: deepSSF Model Training
text:
ConvJointModel
The deepSSF model! A joint habitat–movement model with two heads: 1. Habitat head — a small CNN applied to the spatial window (env layers + tiled scalars) that outputs a per-pixel log-suitability map. 2. Movement head — a dense MLP (fully-connected layer) that takes the scalar covariates and the previous bearing, and produces parameters for a parametric movement kernel (a mixture of wrapped distributions centred on the current location).
The two log-probability surfaces are summed pixel-wise to give the joint predicted probability map for the animal’s next step.


Show code
model = deepssf.ConvJointModel(params).to(DEVICE)
n_params = sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters())
print(f"Model parameters : {n_params:,}")


Model parameters : 36,349



Print the model structure


Show code
print(model)


ConvJointModel(
  (scalar_grid_output): Scalar_to_Grid_Block()
  (conv_habitat): Conv2d_block_spatial(
    (conv2d): Sequential(
      (0): Conv2d(25, 8, kernel_size=(3, 3), stride=(1, 1), padding=(1, 1))
      (1): ReLU()
      (2): Conv2d(8, 8, kernel_size=(3, 3), stride=(1, 1), padding=(1, 1))
      (3): ReLU()
      (4): Conv2d(8, 8, kernel_size=(3, 3), stride=(1, 1), padding=(1, 1))
      (5): ReLU()
      (6): Conv2d(8, 8, kernel_size=(3, 3), stride=(1, 1), padding=(1, 1))
      (7): ReLU()
      (8): Conv2d(8, 8, kernel_size=(3, 3), stride=(1, 1), padding=(1, 1))
      (9): ReLU()
      (10): Conv2d(8, 8, kernel_size=(3, 3), stride=(1, 1), padding=(1, 1))
      (11): ReLU()
      (12): Conv2d(8, 8, kernel_size=(3, 3), stride=(1, 1), padding=(1, 1))
      (13): ReLU()
      (14): Conv2d(8, 1, kernel_size=(3, 3), stride=(1, 1), padding=(1, 1))
    )
  )

    (conv2d): Sequential(
      (0): Conv2d(25, 8, kernel_size=(3, 3), stride=(1, 1), padding=(1, 1))
      (1): ReLU()
      (2): MaxPool2d(kernel_size=2, stride=2, padding=0, dilation=1, ceil_mode=False)
      (3): Conv2d(8, 8, kernel_size=(3, 3), stride=(1, 1), padding=(1, 1))
      (4): ReLU()
      (5): MaxPool2d(kernel_size=2, stride=2, padding=0, dilation=1, ceil_mode=False)
      (6): Conv2d(8, 8, kernel_size=(3, 3), stride=(1, 1), padding=(1, 1))
      (7): ReLU()
      (8): MaxPool2d(kernel_size=2, stride=2, padding=0, dilation=1, ceil_mode=False)
      (9): Conv2d(8, 8, kernel_size=(3, 3), stride=(1, 1), padding=(1, 1))
      (10): ReLU()
      (11): MaxPool2d(kernel_size=2, stride=2, padding=0, dilation=1, ceil_mode=False)
      (12): Flatten(start_dim=1, end_dim=-1)
    )
  )

    (ffn): Sequential(
      (0): Linear(in_features=72, out_features=128, bias=True)
      (1): Dropout(p=0.0, inplace=False)
      (2): ReLU()
      (3): Linear(in_features=128, out_features=128, bias=True)
      (4): Dropout(p=0.0, inplace=False)
      (5): ReLU()
      (6): Linear(in_features=128, out_features=12, bias=True)
    )
  )
  (movement_grid_output): Params_to_Grid_Block_ChV()
)

title: deepSSF Model Training
text:
negativeLogLikeLoss
Scores each predicted probability map against the true next-step pixel index; minimising it pushes probability mass toward observed locations.


Show code
loss_fn = deepssf.negativeLogLikeLoss(reduction="mean")

title: deepSSF Model Training
text:
make_optimisers()
Creates two Adam optimisers with separate learning rates:

lr_habitat

controls the CNN (habitat) head

lr_movement

controls the movement branch (conv_movement + fcn_movement_all), kept lower for stability


It also returns a ReduceLROnPlateau scheduler for each optimiser that reduces the learning rate by a factor of scheduler_factor if that head’s validation loss does not improve for scheduler_patience epochs.
Note that each scheduler now watches its own component of the validation loss. Previously both watched the combined loss, which is dominated by the movement component — so the movement head’s plateau was what cut the habitat learning rate. With that fixed, the two learning rates no longer have to be separated by two orders of magnitude to stop movement from running away with training; start closer together and tune from there.


Show code
optimisers, schedulers = deepssf.make_optimisers(
    model, 
    lr_habitat=5e-5, 
    lr_movement=1e-5, 
    scheduler_patience=3, 
    scheduler_factor=0.5
)

title: deepSSF Model Training
text:
EarlyStopping()
Defines when the model should stop training.

patience

If the loss doesn’t improve for patience epochs, terminate training




Show code
early_stop = deepssf.EarlyStopping(
    patience=10,
    verbose=True,
    monitor="both",                 # stop only when BOTH heads have plateaued
    path=str(OUTPUT_DIR / "best_model.pt"),
    checkpoint_on="active",         # a habitat-only stage saves on habitat loss
    # Also keep each head's own best epoch, across the whole run
    head_paths={
        "habitat":  str(OUTPUT_DIR / "best_model_habitat.pt"),
        "movement": str(OUTPUT_DIR / "best_model_movement.pt"),
    },
)

create_gif()
Assembles the snapshots in snapshot_dir into an animation so you can see how the predictions evolve as training progresses.
Display it with IPython.display.Image, which reads the file and embeds the bytes in the notebook’s output. A hand-written <img src="outputs/....gif"> tag does not work here: the notebook’s HTML output is rendered in a sandboxed webview whose base URL is not the notebook’s directory, so a relative path resolves to nothing and you get an empty box. Nothing is generating a still frame — there is simply no image being loaded at all. Embedding also means the animation survives being exported to HTML or shared as a standalone .ipynb.

Training - loss across epochs


Show code
# Three panels rather than one: the habitat and movement components move on very
# different scales, so sharing an axis would flatten the habitat curve into a
# horizontal line.  x = 0 is the pre-training baseline recorded by fit().
uniform_nll = np.log(WINDOW_SIZE ** 2)
epochs = np.arange(len(history["val_losses"]))
stages = np.asarray(history["stage"])

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(14, 3.6), constrained_layout=True)

panels = [
    ("Combined", history["val_losses"], history["train_losses"]),
    ("Habitat", history["val_habitat_losses"], None),
    ("Movement", history["val_movement_losses"], None),
]

for ax, (title, val, train) in zip(axes, panels):
    if train is not None:
        ax.plot(epochs, train, color="0.6", lw=1.5, label="train")
    ax.plot(epochs, val, color="C0", lw=1.5, label="val")
    if title == "Habitat":
        # A uniform surface over the window scores log(H*W), so this line is the
        # "learned nothing" mark — the whole question for the habitat head is how
        # far below it the curve gets.  Movement sits far below it from the first
        # epoch, and drawing it there would only compress that panel's axis.
        ax.axhline(uniform_nll, color="0.4", ls="--", lw=1,
                   label=f"uniform ({uniform_nll:.2f})")
    # Shade the staged-training blocks so the schedule is readable off the curve.
    for s in np.unique(stages[stages >= 0])[1::2]:
        within = epochs[stages == s]
        ax.axvspan(within.min() - 0.5, within.max() + 0.5, color="0.92", zorder=0)
    ax.set_xlabel("Epoch (0 = untrained baseline)")
    ax.set_ylabel("NLL (nats)")
    ax.set_title(title)
    ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8)
    ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)

fig.suptitle("Training history — combined loss and its two components")
plt.savefig(str(OUTPUT_DIR / "loss_history.png"), dpi=100)
plt.show()

title: deepSSF Model Training
text:
Choosing which checkpoint to use
fit() leaves the model holding its final-epoch weights, not the best ones, so load a checkpoint before testing or simulating.

best_model.pt — the model to use for simulation. Both heads from one epoch, so the joint likelihood is the one that was actually measured.
best_model_habitat.pt / best_model_movement.pt — each head at its own best epoch, tracked across the whole run.

Mixing them is a deliberate trade: taking the habitat head from a different epoch gives the sharpest habitat surface to map, but the two heads then come from different epochs and the joint model’s likelihood is no longer what either checkpoint recorded. Use it for the landscape predictions below, not for simulating trajectories.


Show code
# The joint model — what the simulations further down should use
ckpt = deepssf.load_checkpoint(str(OUTPUT_DIR / "best_model.pt"), model)
print(f"best_model.pt         saved on '{ckpt['checkpoint_criterion']}' "
      f"= {ckpt['checkpoint_score']:.6f}")

hab_ckpt = deepssf.load_checkpoint(str(OUTPUT_DIR / "best_model_habitat.pt"))
print(f"best_model_habitat.pt  saved on '{hab_ckpt['checkpoint_criterion']}' "
      f"= {hab_ckpt['checkpoint_score']:.6f}")

# How much habitat was left on the table by the last epoch.  The two numbers
# above are different quantities (a combined loss and a habitat loss) and are
# not comparable directly, so read the gap off the history instead.
hab_hist = np.asarray(history["val_habitat_losses"])
best_epoch = int(np.nanargmin(hab_hist))
print(f"\nhabitat NLL: best {hab_hist[best_epoch]:.4f} at epoch {best_epoch}, "
      f"final {hab_hist[-1]:.4f} — a gap of {hab_hist[-1] - hab_hist[best_epoch]:+.4f} nats")
print(f"(a uniform surface over the window scores {np.log(WINDOW_SIZE ** 2):.4f} - "
      f"a gap of {hab_hist[-1] - np.log(WINDOW_SIZE ** 2):+.4f}.")

# To map the sharpest habitat surface instead, overwrite just that head:
# load_head_weights(str(OUTPUT_DIR / "best_model_habitat.pt"), model, "habitat")

section: Convert the NumPy rasters loaded earlier into PyTorch tensors.
text:
Convert the NumPy rasters loaded earlier into PyTorch tensors.
Both validate_next_step_probs() and simulate_trajectory() call get_landscape(month_index) at each step to fetch the current environmental layers as a list of 2-D tensors.
With static (non-seasonal) rasters the month_index argument is unused. For seasonal data (e.g. monthly NDVI composites) you would index into a stack of layers here based on the current month.


Show code
# validate_next_step_probs() and simulate_trajectory() both stack the list returned
# by get_landscape() along a new channel dimension, so every element must be a *2-D*
# tensor.  Unbind the band dimension of any multi-band layer so the channel order
# matches what MovementDataset fed the model during training.
landscape_tensors = []
for arr in env_layers.values():
    t = torch.from_numpy(np.asarray(arr).astype(np.float32))
    landscape_tensors.extend([t] if t.ndim == 2 else list(t))

print(f"Landscape channels: {len(landscape_tensors)}  (each {tuple(landscape_tensors[0].shape)})")

def get_landscape(_month_index):
    # Returns one 2-D tensor per spatial channel, in the same order as LAYER_PATHS.
    return landscape_tensors

# Take the last 10 % of steps as a test sample.  CAVEAT: make_dataloaders() uses a
# random_split, so these steps were mostly *seen during training* — the numbers below
# are not a clean out-of-sample estimate.  Because step_df is ordered by individual
# name, this slice is also just the last few pigs alphabetically rather than the
# latest steps in time.  Hold out individuals or a date range explicitly for a real test.
n_test      = int(len(step_df) * 0.1)
test_sample = step_df.iloc[-n_test:].reset_index(drop=True)
print(f"Testing on {len(test_sample):,} steps")

title: deepSSF Model Training
text:
validate_next_step_probs()
Runs the model forward on each test step and records the probability mass assigned to the true next location.

Inputs:

model
test_sample

test dataframe that contains movement steps (from the data loaded above)

get_landscape

retrieves the landscape layers (spatial covariates) that were used to train the model

transform

raster Affine transform

window_size

window size of the local availability window (should be the same as for training)

scalar_cols

scalar column names (should be set from above)

yday_col

which column has the yday column to ensure the correct spatial layers (if dynamic through time) are indexed

month_index_fn

a function mapping day-of-year → month index (used by the get_landscape function). Here we are using static spatial layers so we can set it to 0.


Outputs:

test_sample dataframe with three new columns appended:

habitat_prob — probability at the true location from the habitat head alone
move_prob — probability at the true location from the movement head alone
next_step_prob — joint (habitat × movement) probability at the true location



Higher values mean the model performed better (there was higher predicted probability at the observed next-step).


Show code
# Use the last 10 % of steps as the test set (matches the DataLoader split)
n_test      = int(len(step_df) * 0.1)
test_sample = step_df.iloc[-n_test:].reset_index(drop=True)
print(f"Validating on {len(test_sample):,} steps")

val_results = deepssf.validate_next_step_probs(
    model,
    test_sample,
    get_landscape=get_landscape,
    transform=raster_transform,
    window_size=WINDOW_SIZE,
    scalar_cols=tuple(SCALAR_COLS),
    yday_col="yday_t1",
    bearing_col="bearing_tm1",
    month_index_fn=lambda _yday: 0,   # static layers — month doesn't matter
)
print(val_results[["habitat_prob", "move_prob", "next_step_prob"]].describe())

Set random seed and the device for predicting from the model
If you have a GPU, this is where it will be specified (automatically).

# Reproducibility — fix random seeds so results are the same on every run.

title: deepSSF Predictions
text:
Set script paths
These must point at the same data and rasters the model was trained on — the model takes one input channel per raster band, in LAYER_PATHS order, so a different set of layers (or a different order) either fails to load the weights or feeds the wrong covariate into each filter.
OUTPUT_DIR is the directory a training run wrote its checkpoints to, given here as a literal path rather than through get_output_dir() (which mints a new dated directory). Figures and rasters produced below are written back into the same directory, alongside the model they came from.
All-caps names below are module-level constants — set once here and referenced throughout the notebook without being reassigned. Python has no built-in constant keyword, so capitalisation is the community convention (PEP 8) to signal “do not change this value”.


Show code
DATA_DIR = Path("data")  # location of the bundled sample data
MAPPING_DIR = Path("mapping")  # location of the landcover mapping files
CSV_PATH = DATA_DIR / "pigs_east_alligator_steps_covs_20261015.csv"  # GPS tracking data, 28 individuals

# Must match LAYER_PATHS in deepssf_piggies_train_landcover.ipynb, in the same order.
# NOTE: 's2' and 's2_dir' are RESERVED keys in load_environmental_layers().
# 's2_dir' triggers the monthly-composite loader (load_s2_data), and a plain
# 's2' entry is skipped by the per-file loop — so a single multi-band GeoTIFF
# must be given any *other* name, otherwise nothing is loaded and the function
# raises "raster_transform could not be set".
LAYER_PATHS = {
    # Topographic layers (DEM, slope)
    "dem": str(MAPPING_DIR / "DEM_east_alligator_3112.tif"),
    "slope": str(MAPPING_DIR / "slope_east_alligator_3112.tif"),

    # Categorical landcover layers (one-hot encoded)
    "landcover": str(MAPPING_DIR / "landcover_dummy_east_alligator.tif"),
}

# The training run to predict from — where its checkpoints and scaling
# coefficients were written by deepssf_piggies_train_landcover.ipynb, and where
# the outputs below are saved.
OUTPUT_DIR = Path("outputs/landcover/2026-11-17_1")
CKPT_PATH = OUTPUT_DIR / "best_model.pt"
SCALING_PATH = OUTPUT_DIR / "scalar_scaling.csv"  # weather-covariate scaling used in training

for path in (CKPT_PATH, SCALING_PATH):
    if not path.exists():
        raise FileNotFoundError(
            f"No {path.name} in {OUTPUT_DIR} — set OUTPUT_DIR to a directory that "
            "deepssf_piggies_train_landcover.ipynb has finished writing to."
        )
print(f"Output directory: {OUTPUT_DIR}")
print("Checkpoints:", ", ".join(sorted(p.name for p in OUTPUT_DIR.glob("*.pt"))))

Checkpoints: best_model.pt, best_model_habitat.pt, best_model_movement.pt

title: deepSSF Predictions
text:
load_environmental_layers()
Reads each GeoTIFF listed in LAYER_PATHS, min–max

Scales every band to [0, 1], and returns:

env_layers — dict mapping layer name → NumPy array: 2-D (H × W) for single-band GeoTIFFs, 3-D (bands × H × W) for multi-band ones, where each band becomes its own model input channel
raster_transform — Affine object that converts pixel (row, col) indices to the projected coordinates (easting, northing) of the raster(s), which should be in the same CRS as the GPS data. This transform is used whenever we need to translate between pixel space and real-world coordinates.


Two things to watch for:

The keys 's2' and 's2_dir' are reserved for the monthly Sentinel-2 composite loader — a single GeoTIFF passed under the name 's2' is silently skipped (see the note in the paths cell above).
The rescaling uses a single global min/max across all bands of a file, and computes (data - lo) / hi rather than (data - lo) / (hi - lo). Our index raster is int16 scaled by 10 000 with ±10 000 fill values, so the loaded values span [0, 2] rather than [0, 1] and the three indices are not individually normalised. That is workable (the CNN can rescale internally) but if it hurts training, pre-scale each band yourself and save as .npy — non-.tif paths in LAYER_PATHS are loaded with np.load(..., mmap_mode='r') and left untouched, though at least one real .tif must remain in the dict so the transform can be set.



Show code
env_layers, raster_transform = deepssf.load_environmental_layers(LAYER_PATHS)
print("Layers loaded:", list(env_layers.keys()))
for name, arr in env_layers.items():
    print(f"  {name}: shape={arr.shape}, min={arr.min():.3f}, max={arr.max():.3f}")

# Each band of a multi-band layer becomes one CNN input channel, so count bands
# (not layers) here and reuse the total when setting ModelParams below.  Deriving
# it means switching rasters in LAYER_PATHS needs no other edits.
N_SPATIAL_CHANNELS = sum(1 if arr.ndim == 2 else arr.shape[0] for arr in env_layers.values())
print(f"Spatial channels: {N_SPATIAL_CHANNELS}")

title: deepSSF Predictions
text:
SCALAR_COLS
These are non-spatial inputs. For processing with convolutional layers, they are converted into spatial windows (rasters/arrays), and stacked with the truly spatial covariates.
The model receives a fixed-size spatial window centred on each step’s start location. To let the network express time-varying habitat preferences (e.g. different nocturnal vs diurnal use), scalar covariates are tiled into additional channels of the same H × W size, so every pixel “knows” the current time context when habitat suitability is estimated.

hour_t1_sin1 / hour_t1_cos1

Sine and cosine of (2π × hour / 24), encoding time-of-day as a circular variable. The circular encoding means 23:00 and 01:00 are treated as adjacent — a plain hour value would have an artificial discontinuity at midnight.

yday_t1_sin1 / yday_t1_cos1

Same circular encoding for day-of-year (1–365), capturing seasonal variation in habitat use (e.g. dry-season vs wet-season movements).

dt_hour

Elapsed time between consecutive fixes (hours). Because GPS collars do not always fix at a perfectly regular rate, including dt_hour lets the movement kernel rescale expected displacement proportionally to the actual time interval rather than assuming a fixed fix rate. Note: dt_hour must be supplied at simulation time as well, so that simulate_trajectory() produces inputs consistent with training.

Weather covariates from the onpli_ weather station, carried over from the CSV for the start of each step:

rain_30min_mm, air_temp_c, wet_bulb_temp_c, dew_point_temp_c, rel_humidity_pct, wind_speed_kmh

Standardised to z-scores (the *_scaled columns) before going into the model, with rain log-transformed, log(1 + x), first. The mean and SD are kept so model inputs and effects can be converted back to natural units.

wind_dir_deg

Encoded as a sine/cosine pair (onpli_wind_dir_sin1 / onpli_wind_dir_cos1) for the same wraparound reason as hour of day, with calm steps set to (0, 0).



These must match SCALAR_COLS in the training notebook — same columns, same order.


Show code
# Time covariates derived by prepare_movement_df().  Not scaled: the sin/cos pairs
# are already in [-1, 1], and simulate_trajectory() fills dt_hour with the raw
# time_between_steps (hours), so the model has to be trained on raw hours too.
TIME_COLS = ["hour_t1_sin1",
             "hour_t1_cos1",
             "yday_t1_sin1",
             "yday_t1_cos1",
             "dt_hour"]

# Weather covariates carried over from the CSV in natural units, and standardised
# to z-scores further down (the "_scaled" columns)
WEATHER_COLS = ["onpli_rain_30min_mm",
                "onpli_air_temp_c",
                "onpli_wet_bulb_temp_c",
                "onpli_dew_point_temp_c",
                "onpli_rel_humidity_pct",
                "onpli_wind_speed_kmh"
                ]

prepare_movement_df()
Converts a fixes dataframe (one row per GPS location) into a step dataframe (one row per movement between consecutive fixes).

For each step it computes:

dx, dy — displacement in projected CRS units (metres)
bearing — direction of travel (radians; 0 = north, clockwise positive)
bearing_tm1 — bearing of the previous step, used as a model input so the network can capture directional persistence by estimating a turning angle
dt_hour — time elapsed between consecutive fixes (hours)
hour_t1, yday_t1 — decimal hour-of-day and day-of-year at the step start location
*_sin1 / *_cos1 — sine/cosine encodings of hour and yday (see SCALAR_COLS below)


The “1” on column names (x1_, y1_, t1_, etc.) flags them as “start of step” variables; and the “2” in x2_, y2_, t2_ are the corresponding “end of step” values, following the convention of the amt package (Signer et al. 2019). The last fix for each individual is dropped because no forward step can be formed.


Show code

# let it re-form the steps from consecutive fixes.

Encode wind direction as a sin/cos pair
Wind direction follows the BoM convention: the compass bearing the wind blows from, in 10° steps clockwise from north (90 = from the east). North is recorded as 360, and 0 is reserved for calm (no wind, so no direction).
Taking the sine and cosine removes the wraparound, so 350° and 10° sit next to each other and 0° and 360° both mean north: - onpli_wind_dir_sin1 — east–west component (+1 = from the east, −1 = from the west) - onpli_wind_dir_cos1 — north–south component (+1 = from the north, −1 = from the south)
Calm steps are set to (0, 0). A plain sin/cos of 0° gives (0, 1), which the model would read as a northerly. wind_dir_from_sin_cos() converts back to 0–360° (0 = north), returning NaN for calm.


Show code
def wind_dir_to_sin_cos(deg):
    """Compass degrees (0 = north, clockwise) -> (sin, cos)."""
    rad = np.radians(np.asarray(deg, dtype=float))
    return np.sin(rad), np.cos(rad)


def wind_dir_from_sin_cos(sin1, cos1):
    """(sin, cos) -> compass degrees in [0, 360), 0 = north.  NaN for calm (0, 0)."""
    sin1 = np.asarray(sin1, dtype=float)
    cos1 = np.asarray(cos1, dtype=float)
    # Round before wrapping so north comes back as 0 rather than 359.99999...
    deg = np.round(np.degrees(np.arctan2(sin1, cos1)), 6) % 360
    return np.where(np.hypot(sin1, cos1) < 1e-6, np.nan, deg)


calm = (step_df[WIND_DIR_COL] == 0).to_numpy()   # BoM code for calm
wind_sin, wind_cos = wind_dir_to_sin_cos(step_df[WIND_DIR_COL])
step_df["onpli_wind_dir_sin1"] = np.where(calm, 0.0, wind_sin)
step_df["onpli_wind_dir_cos1"] = np.where(calm, 0.0, wind_cos)

Scale the weather covariates with the training coefficients
The model was trained on weather covariates scaled with a particular transform, mean and SD (rain log-transformed, log(1 + x), then every covariate converted to a z-score). Any input to the model has to be scaled the same way, so the coefficients are loaded from scalar_scaling.csv, which the training notebook saved in OUTPUT_DIR, rather than recalculated here.

scale_covariate(values, col) converts natural units to the model’s scale, e.g. for weather values set by hand for a prediction.
unscale_covariate(values, col) converts back to natural units: natural = scaled × SD + mean, followed by exp(x) − 1 for log1p columns.

As a check, the coefficients are also recalculated from the data loaded here. They should match, unless the data or the NA handling has changed since the model was trained.


Show code
# Transform, mean and SD for each weather covariate, as used in training
SCALING = pd.read_csv(SCALING_PATH, index_col="column")
missing = [col for col in WEATHER_COLS if col not in SCALING.index]
if missing:
    raise KeyError(f"{SCALING_PATH} has no scaling for {missing}")
print("Scaling coefficients (from training):")
print(SCALING.round(3).to_string())


def scale_covariate(values, col):
    """Natural units -> model scale for `col`: log1p if listed, then z-score."""
    values = np.asarray(values, dtype=float)
    if SCALING.at[col, "transform"] == "log1p":
        values = np.log1p(values)
    return (values - SCALING.at[col, "mean"]) / SCALING.at[col, "sd"]


def unscale_covariate(values, col):
    """Model scale -> natural units for `col`: undo the z-score, then expm1 if logged."""
    values = np.asarray(values, dtype=float) * SCALING.at[col, "sd"] + SCALING.at[col, "mean"]
    if SCALING.at[col, "transform"] == "log1p":
        values = np.expm1(values)
    return values


for col in WEATHER_COLS:
    step_df[f"{col}_scaled"] = scale_covariate(step_df[col], col)

# Check: recalculating the coefficients from this notebook's data gives the same
# values as the training run
for col in WEATHER_COLS:
    values = step_df[col].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    if SCALING.at[col, "transform"] == "log1p":
        values = np.log1p(values)
    if not np.allclose([values.mean(), values.std(ddof=1)],
                       SCALING.loc[col, ["mean", "sd"]].to_numpy(dtype=float)):
        print(f"Warning: {col} mean/SD differ from training — has the data or NA "
              "handling changed since the model was trained?")
        break
else:
    print("\nCoefficients recalculated from this data match the training run.")

filter_steps_by_window()
Removes steps whose straight-line displacement exceeds half the spatial window (WINDOW_SIZE × PIXEL_SIZE / 2 metres). Such steps would place the true next location outside the predicted probability map, causing an index error in the loss function.

title: deepSSF Predictions
text:
params_from_checkpoint()
Weights only load into a model built with the same architecture, so predicting from a trained model means reproducing its hyper-parameters exactly. Rather than re-typing the training notebook’s constants here — where a habitat branch one layer too shallow fails loudly, but a mis-set pixel_size quietly rescales the movement kernel — params_from_checkpoint() recovers them from the checkpoint and returns the ModelParams to hand to ConvJointModel.
deepssf writes the ModelParams dict into every checkpoint, so for a model trained with 0.3.1 or later it is simply read back. Older checkpoints (anything in outputs/ trained before then) do not have it, and the architecture is recovered from the layer shapes instead: a conv weight is [out_channels, in_channels, k, k] and a linear weight [out_features, in_features], which between them pin down every hyper-parameter that changes a tensor shape — input_channels, output_channels, kernel_size, both conv-layer counts, dense_dim_in_all, dense_dim_hidden and num_movement_params. Either way the result is checked against the saved tensors, so a stored params dict that contradicts its own weights raises here rather than failing later inside load_state_dict.
Three things it cannot get from the file, passed in below:

image_dim — the habitat branch is fully convolutional, so nothing in the weights records the training window. The movement branch’s flattened size does constrain it, and that is checked, but only to within the slack that max-pooling’s floor division allows (48–55 px all flatten to the same 288 here). WINDOW_SIZE also has to match filter_steps_by_window() above, and is the window the simulations step within.
pixel_size — a property of the raster, read off raster_transform.
device — where the model is being run, which has nothing to do with where it was trained; it defaults to this machine rather than to the recorded value.

n_scalar_covariates only fills the two ModelParams fields that no layer reads; the scalar count that matters is folded into input_channels, which comes off the weights. The check below is the one thing the checkpoint cannot do for us — that the covariates loaded in this notebook are the ones the model was trained on. It compares counts only, so keep LAYER_PATHS in the training run’s order.


Show code
params = deepssf.params_from_checkpoint(
    str(CKPT_PATH),
    image_dim=WINDOW_SIZE,               # not recorded in the weights
    pixel_size=PIXEL_SIZE,               # from raster_transform
    n_scalar_covariates=len(SCALAR_COLS),
    device=DEVICE,                       # this machine, not the training machine
)
for name, value in params.to_dict().items():
    print(f"  {name:26s}: {value}")

# The covariates in this notebook must be the ones the model was trained on.
# input_channels is one channel per raster band plus one per scalar covariate,
# so a changed LAYER_PATHS or SCALAR_COLS shows up here as a count mismatch.
n_expected = N_SPATIAL_CHANNELS + len(SCALAR_COLS)
if n_expected != params.input_channels:
    raise ValueError(
        f"{N_SPATIAL_CHANNELS} raster bands + {len(SCALAR_COLS)} scalars = {n_expected} "
        f"input channels, but the checkpoint was trained with {params.input_channels}. "
        "LAYER_PATHS or SCALAR_COLS differ from the training run."
    )
print(f"\n{N_SPATIAL_CHANNELS} raster bands + {len(SCALAR_COLS)} scalars = "
      f"{params.input_channels} input channels - matches the checkpoint")

title: deepSSF Predictions
text:
ConvJointModel
The deepSSF model! A joint habitat–movement model with two heads: 1. Habitat head — a small CNN applied to the spatial window (env layers + tiled scalars) that outputs a per-pixel log-suitability map. 2. Movement head — a dense MLP (fully-connected layer) that takes the scalar covariates and the previous bearing, and produces parameters for a parametric movement kernel (a mixture of wrapped distributions centred on the current location).
The two log-probability surfaces are summed pixel-wise to give the joint predicted probability map for the animal’s next step.


Show code
model = deepssf.ConvJointModel(params).to(DEVICE)
n_params = sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters())
print(f"Model parameters : {n_params:,}")


Model parameters : 36,349

title: deepSSF Predictions
text:
Load the trained model
ConvJointModel above is freshly initialised — random weights — so nothing it predicts means anything until a checkpoint is loaded into it. A training run writes three:

best_model.pt — the model to use for simulation. Both heads from one epoch, so the joint likelihood is the one that was actually measured.
best_model_habitat.pt / best_model_movement.pt — each head at its own best epoch, tracked across the whole run.

Mixing them is a deliberate trade: taking the habitat head from a different epoch gives the sharpest habitat surface to map, but the two heads then come from different epochs and the joint model’s likelihood is no longer what either checkpoint recorded. Use it for the landscape predictions below, not for simulating trajectories.
load_checkpoint() loads the weights in place and is strict about shapes, so a mismatch between the constants set above and the trained architecture raises here rather than silently predicting from a partly-random model.


Show code
# The joint model — what the simulations further down should use
ckpt = deepssf.load_checkpoint(str(CKPT_PATH), model)
print(f"best_model.pt          saved on '{ckpt['checkpoint_criterion']}' "
      f"= {ckpt['checkpoint_score']:.6f}")
print(f"                       trained with deepssf {ckpt.get('deepssf_version', 'unknown')}, "
      f"val_loss {ckpt['val_loss']:.6f}")

hab_ckpt = deepssf.load_checkpoint(str(OUTPUT_DIR / "best_model_habitat.pt"))
print(f"best_model_habitat.pt  saved on '{hab_ckpt['checkpoint_criterion']}' "
      f"= {hab_ckpt['checkpoint_score']:.6f}")
print(f"(a uniform surface over the window scores {np.log(WINDOW_SIZE ** 2):.4f})")

# Prediction only — no gradients needed, and this turns off dropout/batchnorm
# training behaviour.
model.eval()

# To map the sharpest habitat surface instead, overwrite just that head:
# load_head_weights(str(OUTPUT_DIR / "best_model_habitat.pt"), model, "habitat")

                       trained with deepssf 0.3.2, val_loss 4.009099

(a uniform surface over the window scores 7.8637)

  (conv_habitat): Conv2d_block_spatial(
    (conv2d): Sequential(
      (0): Conv2d(25, 8, kernel_size=(3, 3), stride=(1, 1), padding=(1, 1))
      (1): ReLU()
      (2): Conv2d(8, 8, kernel_size=(3, 3), stride=(1, 1), padding=(1, 1))
      (3): ReLU()
      (4): Conv2d(8, 8, kernel_size=(3, 3), stride=(1, 1), padding=(1, 1))
      (5): ReLU()
      (6): Conv2d(8, 8, kernel_size=(3, 3), stride=(1, 1), padding=(1, 1))
      (7): ReLU()
      (8): Conv2d(8, 8, kernel_size=(3, 3), stride=(1, 1), padding=(1, 1))
      (9): ReLU()
      (10): Conv2d(8, 8, kernel_size=(3, 3), stride=(1, 1), padding=(1, 1))
      (11): ReLU()
      (12): Conv2d(8, 8, kernel_size=(3, 3), stride=(1, 1), padding=(1, 1))
      (13): ReLU()
      (14): Conv2d(8, 1, kernel_size=(3, 3), stride=(1, 1), padding=(1, 1))
    )
  )
  (conv_movement): Conv2d_block_toFC(
    (conv2d): Sequential(
      (0): Conv2d(25, 8, kernel_size=(3, 3), stride=(1, 1), padding=(1, 1))
      (1): ReLU()
      (2): MaxPool2d(kernel_size=2, stride=2, padding=0, dilation=1, ceil_mode=False)
      (3): Conv2d(8, 8, kernel_size=(3, 3), stride=(1, 1), padding=(1, 1))
      (4): ReLU()

section: Convert the NumPy rasters loaded earlier into PyTorch tensors
text:
Convert the NumPy rasters loaded earlier into PyTorch tensors
predict_habitat_landscape(), simulate_trajectory() and simulate_trajectories() all call get_landscape(month_index) to fetch the current environmental layers as a list of 2-D tensors.
With static (non-seasonal) rasters the month_index argument is unused. For seasonal data (e.g. monthly NDVI composites) you would index into a stack of layers here based on the current month.


Show code
# The simulation and prediction functions stack the list returned by
# get_landscape() along a new channel dimension, so every element must be a *2-D*
# tensor.  Unbind the band dimension of any multi-band layer so the channel order
# matches what MovementDataset fed the model during training.
landscape_tensors = []
for arr in env_layers.values():
    t = torch.from_numpy(np.asarray(arr).astype(np.float32))
    landscape_tensors.extend([t] if t.ndim == 2 else list(t))

print(f"Landscape channels: {len(landscape_tensors)}  (each {tuple(landscape_tensors[0].shape)})")


def get_landscape(_month_index):
    # Returns one 2-D tensor per spatial channel, in the same order as LAYER_PATHS.
    return landscape_tensors

title: deepSSF Predictions
text:
Scalar inputs for the prediction
The model needs a value for every column in SCALAR_COLS, in that order: - Time (hour_t1_*, yday_t1_*, dt_hour) - deepssf.make_simulation_inputs() builds the sin/cos encodings from a day of the year (PRED_YDAY, integer) and a fractional hour (PRED_HOUR, float). Its time_between_steps argument becomes the dt_hour input, so it is set to the collars’ ~30 min fix interval (PRED_DT_HOUR) rather than left at its default of 1 hour. - Weather (*_scaled) - set by hand in natural units in PRED_WEATHER, then scaled with the coefficients stored in SCALING. - Wind direction (onpli_wind_dir_sin1 / _cos1) - set in degrees in PRED_WIND_DIR_DEG (0 or 360 = north, the direction the wind blows from), and encoded as a sin/cos pair, or (0, 0) when the wind speed is 0 (calm).
Weather varies a lot with season and time of day, so the first cell summarises the training data, both overall and for steps near the chosen moment, as a guide to realistic values. make_scalar_row() then assembles the full row, warning about any weather value outside the training range.


Show code
# Predict for one moment in time: 9:30 am on day 200.
PRED_YDAY = 200  # day of the year to predict for (1–365, integer)
PRED_HOUR = 9.5  # hour of the day to predict for (0–24, float)

# Steps "near" the chosen moment: within ±15 days and ±1 hour, wrapping across
# the new year and midnight
NEAR_DAYS, NEAR_HOURS = 15, 1
yday_diff = (step_df["yday_t1"] - PRED_YDAY + 182.5) % 365 - 182.5
hour_diff = (step_df["hour_t1"] - PRED_HOUR + 12) % 24 - 12
near = (yday_diff.abs() <= NEAR_DAYS) & (hour_diff.abs() <= NEAR_HOURS)

print("Model inputs needed (SCALAR_COLS):")
for col in SCALAR_COLS:
    if col in TIME_COLS:
        source = "PRED_YDAY / PRED_HOUR / PRED_DT_HOUR"
    elif col.endswith("_scaled"):
        source = f'PRED_WEATHER["{col.removesuffix("_scaled")}"]'
    else:
        source = "PRED_WIND_DIR_DEG"
    print(f"  {col:<32} <- {source}")

# Weather in natural units: the full training range, and typical values near the
# chosen moment
near_weather = step_df.loc[near, WEATHER_COLS]
weather_summary = pd.DataFrame({
    "min":        step_df[WEATHER_COLS].min(),
    "mean":       step_df[WEATHER_COLS].mean(),
    "max":        step_df[WEATHER_COLS].max(),
    "near_5%":    near_weather.quantile(0.05),
    "near_median": near_weather.median(),
    "near_95%":   near_weather.quantile(0.95),
})
print(f"\nWeather, all steps vs the {near.sum():,} steps within ±{NEAR_DAYS} days "
      f"and ±{NEAR_HOURS} h of day {PRED_YDAY}, {PRED_HOUR:g} h:")
print(weather_summary.round(2).to_string())

# Wind direction is circular, so a mean is meaningless: show the most common
# directions instead (0 = calm is counted separately)
near_dir = step_df.loc[near, WIND_DIR_COL]
print(f"\nWind direction near the chosen moment: {(near_dir == 0).mean():.0%} calm; "
      "most common directions (deg from north, % of non-calm steps):")
print((near_dir[near_dir > 0].value_counts(normalize=True).head(5) * 100).round(1).to_string())

Show code
# Weather for the prediction, in natural units.  The defaults are roughly the
# medians near day 200 at 09:30 (dry-season mornings).  Temperature, wet bulb,
# dew point and humidity are physically linked, so change them together, e.g. by
# taking them from the same row of the summary above.
PRED_WEATHER = {
    "onpli_rain_30min_mm":    0.0,
    "onpli_air_temp_c":       27.0,
    "onpli_wet_bulb_temp_c":  19.8,
    "onpli_dew_point_temp_c": 15.0,
    "onpli_rel_humidity_pct": 47.0,
    "onpli_wind_speed_kmh":   15.0,
}

# Direction the wind blows FROM, in degrees clockwise from north (0 or 360 =
# north).  Ignored when the wind speed is 0, which is encoded as calm.
PRED_WIND_DIR_DEG = 110.0

# Hours between steps, which is also the model's dt_hour input.  The collars fixed
# about every 30 min, so values far from 0.5 are outside what the model saw.
PRED_DT_HOUR = 0.5


def make_scalar_row(yday, hour, weather=None, wind_dir_deg=None, dt_hour=None):
    """One row of model inputs, in SCALAR_COLS order, from natural-unit values.

    Defaults to PRED_WEATHER, PRED_WIND_DIR_DEG and PRED_DT_HOUR.  Prints a
    warning for any weather value outside the range seen in training.
    """
    weather = PRED_WEATHER if weather is None else weather
    wind_dir_deg = PRED_WIND_DIR_DEG if wind_dir_deg is None else wind_dir_deg
    dt_hour = PRED_DT_HOUR if dt_hour is None else dt_hour

    missing = [col for col in WEATHER_COLS if col not in weather]
    if missing:
        raise KeyError(f"weather is missing {missing}")

    # Time: same encodings the simulation uses, in TIME_COLS order
    time_row = deepssf.make_simulation_inputs(
        n_steps=1, starting_yday=yday, starting_hour=hour, time_between_steps=dt_hour,
    )[0][0]
    values = dict(zip(TIME_COLS, time_row, strict=True))

    # Weather: scaled with the training coefficients
    for col in WEATHER_COLS:
        lo, hi = step_df[col].min(), step_df[col].max()
        if not lo <= weather[col] <= hi:
            print(f"Warning: {col} = {weather[col]} is outside the training range ({lo} to {hi})")
        values[f"{col}_scaled"] = scale_covariate([weather[col]], col)[0]

    # Wind direction: sin/cos, or (0, 0) for calm
    if weather["onpli_wind_speed_kmh"] == 0:
        wind_sin, wind_cos = 0.0, 0.0
    else:
        wind_sin, wind_cos = wind_dir_to_sin_cos(wind_dir_deg)
    values["onpli_wind_dir_sin1"] = wind_sin
    values["onpli_wind_dir_cos1"] = wind_cos

    return np.array([values[col] for col in SCALAR_COLS], dtype=np.float32)


# Check: rebuilding rows of the training data from their natural-unit values gives
# exactly the model inputs the model was trained on
check_rows = step_df[step_df["yday_t1"] <= 365].sample(200, random_state=1)
for _, row in check_rows.iterrows():
    rebuilt = make_scalar_row(
        row["yday_t1"], row["hour_t1"],
        weather=row[WEATHER_COLS].to_dict(),
        wind_dir_deg=row[WIND_DIR_COL],
        dt_hour=row["dt_hour"],
    )
    assert np.allclose(rebuilt, row[SCALAR_COLS].to_numpy(dtype=float), atol=1e-5), row.name
print(f"make_scalar_row() reproduces the training inputs for {len(check_rows)} sampled steps\n")

scalars_pred = make_scalar_row(PRED_YDAY, PRED_HOUR)
print(f"Model inputs for day {PRED_YDAY}, {PRED_HOUR:g} h:")
print(pd.Series(scalars_pred, index=SCALAR_COLS).round(3).to_string())

title: deepSSF Predictions
text:
predict_habitat_landscape()
Everything so far has run the model on a WINDOW_SIZE crop centred on the animal. But the habitat sub-network is fully convolutional — 3x3 convolutions with stride 1 and padding 1, no pooling and no dense layer — so the same trained filters can be swept across the entire raster in a single pass. Convolution is translation-equivariant, so the value at a pixel is exactly what the model would have produced for a window centred on that pixel.
That gives a landscape-wide habitat selection surface. Read it as a relative ranking of cells: “if the animal were somewhere on this landscape, how attractive is each cell”. It deliberately says nothing about whether the animal could reach a cell in one step — that constraint lives in the movement kernel, which takes no part here. The two are only combined over a local window, which is what simulate_next_step() does.

Inputs:

model

the trained model; only model.conv_habitat is used

landscape_rasters

the spatial covariates as a list of 2-D tensors, in the same order and on the same scaling as training — i.e. exactly what get_landscape() returns

scalars

the scalar covariates for the moment being predicted, in SCALAR_COLS order, as built by make_scalar_row() above. Each value is broadcast to a constant layer covering the whole landscape (the same thing Scalar_to_Grid_Block does for a window — that block can’t be reused here because its output size is fixed to WINDOW_SIZE)

normalise

subtract the log-sum-exp over the whole landscape, making the surface a log-probability that sums to 1 across all valid cells

edge_buffer

how many border pixels to mask as NaN. Defaults to habitat_edge_buffer(model) — the exact width the zero-padding reaches, 1 pixel per habitat conv layer. Those pixels saw padding rather than landscape and are not comparable with the interior

chunk_rows

process this many raster rows at a time. A full-landscape activation is several hundred MB, enough to exhaust a GPU; the chunks overlap by edge_buffer so the result is identical to a single pass


Outputs: a [height, width] NumPy array of log-probabilities, NaN in the border. Take np.exp() for probabilities.



Show code
habitat_log = deepssf.predict_habitat_landscape(
    model,
    landscape_rasters=get_landscape(0),   # static layers → month index 0
    scalars=scalars_pred,
)
print(f"\nSurface {habitat_log.shape}, masked border "
      f"{deepssf.habitat_edge_buffer(model)} px")
print(f"log-probability range: {np.nanmin(habitat_log):.2f} to "
      f"{np.nanmax(habitat_log):.2f}")
print(f"probabilities sum to  : {np.nansum(np.exp(habitat_log)):.4f}")



Surface (1335, 1715), masked border 8 px
log-probability range: -16.46 to -11.17
probabilities sum to  : 1.0000



Plot the landscape-scale habitat selection surface
Plotted on the log scale. Across 9.5 million cells the probabilities are tiny (a uniform surface would give ~1e-7 per cell) and a handful of very attractive cells dominate the linear range, so a linear colour scale washes the whole map out. The colour limits are clipped to percentiles for the same reason.


Show code
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 5.5))

# Percentile limits: a few extreme cells otherwise dominate the colour range
vmin, vmax = np.nanpercentile(habitat_log, [1, 99.9])

rasterio.plot.show(
    habitat_log, transform=raster_transform, ax=axes[0],
    cmap="viridis", vmin=vmin, vmax=vmax,
)
axes[0].set_title(f"Habitat selection (log prob) — yday {PRED_YDAY}, "
                  f"{PRED_HOUR:.0f}:00")

rasterio.plot.show(
    habitat_log, transform=raster_transform, ax=axes[1],
    cmap="viridis", vmin=vmin, vmax=vmax,
)
axes[1].plot(
    step_df["x1_"], step_df["y1_"],
    "r.", alpha=0.25, markersize=0.6, label="observed GPS fixes",
)
axes[1].legend(loc="upper right", markerscale=10)
axes[1].set_title("with observed locations overlaid")

for ax in axes:
    ax.set_xlabel("Easting (m, projected)")
    ax.set_ylabel("Northing (m, projected)")

# One colourbar for both panels
fig.colorbar(axes[0].images[0], ax=axes, shrink=0.8, label="log probability")
plt.savefig(str(OUTPUT_DIR / "habitat_landscape.png"), dpi=120, bbox_inches="tight")
plt.show()
